Weight and BMI improvements were particularly evident in trials focused on obesity, while improvements in glycemic control were especially relevant in trials involving young people with type 2 diabetes. We also found improvement in systolic blood pressure. It is also important to recognize that pediatric GLP-1 use does not represent a single indication or age group. In the United States, certain GLP-1 medications are FDA-approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents starting at age 12, while some GLP-1 receptor agonists are approved for type 2 diabetes starting at age 10. These populations can overlap, since obesity commonly coexists with type 2 diabetes in young people. This makes it important, particularly when interpreting real-world prescribing trends, to understand why the medication was prescribed rather than assuming that every GLP-1 prescription in a young person represents treatment specifically for obesity. The safety picture also requires nuance. Gastrointestinal side effects were more common with GLP-1 medications, which is consistent with what we see in adults. Reassuringly, in the randomized trials we analyzed, we did not find significant differences between GLP-1 medications and placebo in treatment discontinuation, depression, or suicidal thoughts or behaviors. At the same time, absence of a statistically significant safety signal does not mean that every potential risk has been definitively ruled out. The duration and size of existing randomized trials may not be sufficient to characterize uncommon adverse events or outcomes that could emerge with longer-term treatment. There are also important outcomes for which evidence remains limited. For example, eating disorders were not reported as an outcome in the trials included in our analysis, so we cannot draw conclusions from these trials about how GLP-1 treatment may affect disordered eating or eating-disorder risk in young people. This is an area that warrants further investigation. That is why I think the conversation should move beyond whether these drugs are simply “good” or “bad” for children. Obesity itself is a chronic disease with consequences that can accumulate over a lifetime, and effective treatment earlier in life could potentially reduce future metabolic and cardiovascular complications. At the same time, children and adolescents are still growing and developing, and we need better long-term evidence about outcomes such as growth, nutrition, mental health, eating disorders, weight trajectories after treatment discontinuation, and uncommon or delayed adverse effects. This need for evidence is becoming increasingly important as GLP-1 use among young people rises rapidly. Continued real-world evidence will therefore be critical for understanding long-term safety, treatment patterns, and outcomes in children and adolescents who receive these medications. Tahniat Syed A clinical associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and clinical director for the Center for Adolescent and Young Adult Health at the UPMC Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh. I think we know a lot at this point. First of all, the diagnosis of being overweight or having obesity is something that has been well defined. In pediatrics we use growth percentiles to track weight. And those who track above the 95th percentile are considered to be in the obesity range, as opposed to adults, where we use a body mass index and typically over 30. Children are growing and developing. They’re going through puberty. Their height is changing. So many aspects of their lives are changing pretty rapidly. So you want to make sure that you have the correct diagnosis of obesity and that you’re treating the correct thing. And there are a variety of anti-obesity medications, including GLP-1s. A GLP-1 drug, its full name is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. We have receptors all throughout your body, including receptors for GLP-1 in particular. So when you’re stimulating this receptor by providing an agonist, what that’s going to do is that it’s going to help your body to actually secrete more insulin to help you digest food. It will slow down the gastric emptying. That helps you feel more full and also acts at the brain level to help with satisfying your hunger. And then it also does some other things that we’re still learning about. So it helps how your metabolism works and potentially increases that a little bit, and it helps with some impulse control. A lot of times what my patients tell me is that what these drugs really, really help with is, quote unquote, food noise. Without being asked, they’ll comment that it’s quieted their food noise. And we know from the studies that have been conducted since 2021 that these GLP-1 receptor agonists are effective at decreasing weight. We’re seeing meaningful weight loss. Meaningful in the sense that it will help with metabolic conditions if they already have that. And that, in turn, helps in so many other ways. It’s important to remember that GLP-1 medications for adolescence are indicated for obesity. So it’s not indicated for a patient as treatment for an eating disorder. But does someone with obesity have disordered eating? Typically, they do, because that’s what this food noise is. There are different forms of eating disorders. A lot of times when people are referring to, quote, unquote, eating disorders, they’re referring to anorexia nervosa, which is when someone has a severe intentional restriction of calories such that they become very underweight, very undernourished. And that’s actually a thought disorder where they believe that they are bigger than what they are, so they restrict calories further to become smaller. But another eating disorder is called binge eating disorder, and that’s where there may be some overlap of what you find when you’re questioning someone who has obesity. There’s also hyperphagia, which refers to having this internal feeling of like needing to eat more and more. There’s sort of this fine line between hyperphagia and binge eating, and then you can also have obesity. I actually just saw a patient just before I came on the phone with you who came to me for weight management, and she has a binge eating disorder. So I’m treating her binge eating disorder and also uncovered that she has anxiety. Those are the things I’m treating while we get to the point of stabilizing her weight and actually helping her weight to come down a little bit. Alaina Vidmar Medical director of obesity medicine and bariatric surgery at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles. I think first and foremost, it’s important just to acknowledge that pediatric obesity is a complex chronic disease. So we know that it’s not the fault of the young person or their parents; it’s really a sort of difference in their biology, in how their brain controls when they’re hungry and when they’re full and how their body uses their calories for energy. But now we have a growing toolkit of ways to help young people living in larger bodies to achieve greater health over time. It’s really not about the number on the scale or the size of one’s body, but we want to help kids to hopefully prevent things like diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol from developing over time. That toolkit has expanded over the last several years to include oral medications and injectable medications, and it’s continuing to expand over time. So we can really take a shared decision-making model to connect with the patient family and understand what is the best tool for us to use for the patient in front of us, while acknowledging that every medication has a different efficacy and a different side effect profile. We can target and really find the best treatment for the kid we’re taking care of. Certainly we’ve been getting a lot of data quickly over the last few years, which is excellent. But I think the biggest thing we want to understand is: How do we best use the medications for various ages? There are lots of different groups who are studying them in younger kids, teenagers, and just spanning the pediatric lifespan. I also think we want to understand who they work the best for. So are there certain patients who respond better to certain medications, and is there any way to predict which medications are going to have which side effects in which kids? Or the flip of that, can we predict which patients are going to have the best effect from a certain medication? There’s a precision approach that we’re hoping to achieve. We do have to acknowledge that just like pediatric obesity is a really complex chronic disease, disordered eating is also another complex chronic disease, and kids can be living with both of them simultaneously. So we need to be thoughtful stewards of both how we screen and uncover multiple chronic diseases that a young person could be living with, and then also how our treatments could be either a part of treating both of them or uncovering another disease that needs to be taken care of. I think that comes from really thoughtful histories that we take where we learn about patients—what is their own history, their family history? And then we also have to thoughtfully monitor treatment over time, just like you would with any kind of response to a medication. We want to understand how this medication changes your eating behaviors or your relationship with food. That’s something we can gather so we can help make sure our patients have what they need to be successful. Lastly, it would be great to understand how we use these medications long-term. I think a lot of us, when we think about obesity as a complex chronic disease, we understand that there’s going to be a cohort of these young people that might need these medications long-term into adulthood. So what does it look like for them? And then what does it look like to take them into a maintenance period? Maybe you need a treatment dose for several years, and then you decrease to a lower dose or [taper off]. And so I think understanding what those algorithms look like and how best to help support patients and families as they’re traversing that would be very helpful. Giz Asks is a recurring Gizmodo series in which experts answer big questions in their own words, offering a range of perspectives on the ideas, discoveries, and debates that affect our lives and shape our understanding of the world.

item.title: LG Denies Its TVs Are Spying on You (Unless You Opted In)
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.19
LG is pushing back against claims that its TVs eavesdrop on owners constantly after a joint report by Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs discovered unsettling details about how much data it phones home—including when the devices are offline or in standby mode. The report used packet capture and firmware analysis to conclude that a range of LG retail OLED TVs scan local area networks to identify devices like phones and smartwatches, as well as the location data of nearby Wi-Fi networks, for LG Ad Solutions. Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs also said they’d found evidence LG TVs also record audio via their microphones, even when on standby or disconnected, and take samples of audio and video data to identify content for advertisers (Automatic Content Recognition or ACR, which is ubiquitous). In a statement on Saturday, LG wrote that “LG smart TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations.” Instead, the company argued, LG TVs only record voices when users state a wake word or hit a corresponding voice/AI button on a remote control. (“Continuously” is a bit of a weasel word, as the original report contained a clip of an LG TV transcribing ambient conversation long after the authors had stopped addressing it.) “Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, audio is not converted to text, stored, or transmitted,” LG wrote. That process may generate “voice-recognition results and related technical logs,” and TVs may use speech-recognition results “to support voice-related features” but don’t later upload that data if it’s recorded while the TV is offline or disconnected. Finally, LG stated that “Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional” and opt-in on their TVs. It stated its ACR features record audio samples via a TV’s internal audio processor, not a speaker, and “does not collect screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings” from a device. As Pocket Lint noted in its guide to turn off data collection on LG TVs—requiring five separate steps—LG’s “opt-in” process slips itself into the middle of a bunch of user agreements during initial setup. The Next Web argued that European regulators may want to look into whether LG’s consent processes comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy rules, though Americans are probably out of luck. “People often consent to things they don’t fully understand during a speedy setup—they just want to get the thing done and up and working,” Newcastle University Professor of Law, Innovation, and Society Lillian Edwards told TechRadar. Consumer Reports has a rundown on how to disable ACR across most major TV manufacturers, though you could also do what I do: Plug in an Xbox and never connect the TV itself to the internet in the first place.

item.title: Apple May Pivot the Beats Brand Into a Way of Marketing Less Polished Products, Starting With Gamer Gear
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.12
Did you ever drive a Scion? Status-obsessed people may have scoffed at your budget-friendly car, but you probably knew at the time it was just a Toyota with a different nameplate on it. According to a new report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple may be looking to turn the Beats brand into a similar repository for lower-priced goods. A couple weeks ago, hidden code was found, seemingly exposing a secret Apple project aimed at developing gaming controllers—perhaps not unlike some of the cool and fun-to-use third-party accessories that already exist. And Gurman now says his anonymous inside sources have told him Apple “has indeed been working on gaming controllers for the iPhone for a bit over a year.” However, Gurman claims, the controllers Apple has in mind may never carry Apple branding. The controller idea is being developed under the aegis of Beats, Gurman writes. At the same time, he says, Apple has begun to use Beats as a potential spigot for experimental, un-Apple-like product possibilities. You may recall that Beats began as a headphones brand at one time owned by music executive Jimmy Iovine and AI-loving rapper and music producer Dr. Dre., and Apple bought it in 2014 for $3 billion, (in a transaction that was not without its share of drama). Beats does indeed make a ton of good headphones that don’t get quite as much press as AirPods. But Gurman says Apple increasingly sees Beats as a way to “capitalize on the third-party accessories market” more broadly, without impacting the Apple brand. Did you know, for instance, that Beats, and therefore Apple, makes an $18.99 woven USB-C cable? Marketing a gaming controller is tricky if you’re Apple, Gurman says, because in order to sell well, it can’t exactly require the consumer to be at, let’s say, the Vision Pro income level. That means Apple may steer clear of premium materials and high-status finishes that make an Apple product read as an Apple product the second you see it. “The culture and lifestyle around gaming controllers also could fit naturally under the Beats umbrella,” Gurman claims.

item.title: Universal Studios Japan Celebrates Halloween With First R-Rated Attraction
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.75
Theme parks tend to do a little something extra for Halloween, and this year, Universal Studios Japan is doing even more extra for the occasion. With this year being the park’s 25th anniversary, Japanese attendees will get to experience two big horror-focused attractions. First is Zanzō (or Lights Out: Nightmare Isolation), where guests enter a facility that’s researching nightmares. As they’re tasked with getting out of private rooms housing “unescapable situations” with others or on their own, attendees will be “slowly consumed by a fear [with] no end.” As the translated press preview notes, this is the USJ’s first R-18 attraction, and will require a signed waiver before going in. If that doesn’t sound like your thing, Universal Studios Japan also has an attraction based around Capcom’s Resident Evil Requiem. Known as The Dive, parkgoers will explore recreations of the Wrenwood Hotel and Rhodes Hill Chronic Center, two of that game’s major locations. Expect “creatures attacking from every action,” including The Girl and the Kitchen Chef. Resident Evil has been at many a Halloween Horror Night at Universal Studios Japan. The inclusion here isn’t just because the franchise (known locally as Biohazard) turns 30 this year, it’s also to help celebrate the annual event. HHN celebrates two anniversaries this year—the 25th for its Orlando launch in 1991, and its 15th for Singapore’s in 2011. Japan wouldn’t get this until 2012, but the timing’s apparently too good to not celebrate its local 15th a little ahead of schedule. For anyone traveling as the year winds down and headed for Universal Studios Japan, Zanzō will be around until November 8, and Resident Evil Requiem: The Dive until December 27. The former will cost extra to get in, while The Dive is included with admission. Want more io9 news? item.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Calls for Pause in AI Development, Sort Of
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.72
After yet another whirlwind week of AI developers making wild claims about how it could kill the entire human race, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has a pitch: Let’s slow this whole thing down a little. Amodei wrote in a Saturday blog post that while he remains optimistic AI will be the “latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity,” researchers must “pace the frontier” due to risks like rogue AI, use for crime and terrorism, and economic disruption. “Over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence—not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up,” Amodei wrote. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he added. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.” Amodei’s proposed plan has three steps, none of which would constitute much of a slowdown on their own. He asks for AI firms to allow embedded third-party evaluators, to coordinate between each other and governments on safety standards, and for the U.S. government to seek global coordination on AI safety (including with “authoritarian governments,” i.e. China and Russia). Those steps on their own wouldn’t slow down the pace of AI development, so Amodei suggested various possible agreements “in order of increasing difficulty.” Those include a narrow agreement prohibiting the most obviously malicious uses of AI like bioweapons, a broader international agreement to test models before release for “acute risks,” a “speed limit” on recursive self-improvement, and a “full pacing, or even ‘pause,'” on AI development between governments. While Amodei wrote he supported the final option, but suggested it was quite unlikely to happen. Rather convenient for him, no? The Anthropic CEO cited an incident this summer in which a swarm of OpenAI bots attacked competitor Hugging Face as particular reason for caution. Anthropic itself said it would allow third-party evaluators after releasing a report this week admitting its models had hacked other companies or exploited vulnerabilities on at least four occasions. Amodei’s letter follows the resignation of an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, who claimed in a social media post that AI firms are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence.” He added that industry leaders “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” That helped AI doomerism achieve a sort of crescendo this week, with loud opining from developers, scientists and politicians alike. This is the point where we note that AI doomerism is also a shameless marketing device deployed to convince everyone that these firms are all-powerful, their products inescapable, and their victory inevitable. While it’s obvious AI can be dangerous, there is ample room to be skeptical about what is essentially wild speculation. By exaggerating the risk of apocalyptic consequences, AI firms attempt to steer conversation away from their many other questionable business practices. “Being able to comprehend and reliably navigate novel problems in the messy, open systems of the physical world is an obvious prerequisite for AI systems posing a threat on the scale that the doomers propose,” Duke University tech policy researcher Casey Mock told Nature earlier this year. Current-day AI is nowhere near that point. “The burden of proof should really be on those making the claim that we are on a runaway train toward developing a super intelligence that will exterminate humanity,” Mock added. Nature noted that when University College London researchers polled around 4,000 AI researchers for a March preprint study, just 3% responded that “existential risk” was their top worry (far behind malicious use, job impacts, and hype, to name a few). The New York Times noted that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX/Tesla CEO Elon Musk both immediately agreed with the plan on social media, which should make you deeply suspicious about whatever’s going on.

item.title: The New ‘Crystal Lake’ Trailer Promises Plenty of Summer Camp Death and Miasma
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.44
Crystal Lake is just over a month away, and Peacock is here on, uh, Sunday the 13th with a new trailer. It delivers a deeper look at Linda Cardellini’s Pam Voorhees as her motherly grief and rage begin to escalate to machete-toting levels. “A prequel to the Friday the 13th franchise, the series follows single mother Pam Voorhees, who has been unable to shake her grief after her young, sickly son Jason tragically drowned in the town lake almost a year before,” reads the official description. We’re told that the year of Jason’s death is 1971, so we’ll just overlook the fact that “Don’t Fear the Reaper” didn’t release until 1976. “When two strangers arrive at Pam’s door digging into her past, a disturbing chain of events is set into motion, leaving the townspeople of Crystal Lake wondering: just who is Pam Voorhees?” It looks like Pam’s main concern will be “Where is Jason’s body?”—something that will reverberate throughout the Friday the 13th series as her supernaturally empowered son keeps rising back to life in sequel after sequel. Her secretive past also looks to be an intriguing mystery, and we’re curious to learn more about the year-round denizens of summer destination Crystal Lake. Peacock also released some new images, including one of Pam looking especially gruesome. Say, where was that no-nonsense police force when a certain hockey-masked killer was running rampant through the woods? Crystal Lake comes from studio A24 and creator, showrunner, writer, and executive producer Brad Caleb Kane (It: Welcome to Derry). Dividing up directing duties are Michael Lennox, Celine Held and Logan George, and Quyen Tran. Along with Cardellini, the main cast includes William Catlett (Black Lightning), Devin Kessler, Cameron Scoggins, and Gwendolyn Sundstrom; the recurring cast includes a veteran of Chucky; he plays the young Jason Voorhees), Nick Cordileone, Joy Suprano, Danielle Kotch, and Phoenix Parnevik. Crystal Lake arrives on Peacock starting Thursday, October 15. It’s a binge drop, so you’ll be able to watch all eight episodes at once. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: The ‘V/H/S: SCP’ Movie Doesn’t Involve the Actual SCP Foundation
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.11
Earlier this summer, we learned the V/H/S movies were expanding with a movie focused on the SCP Foundation. As it turns out, things are more complicated than that initial announcement. On Friday, Deadline announced A24 gained worldwide rights to the SCP movie and planned to give it a global theatrical release. Yes, Backrooms has been a hit this year, but the studio’s had other winners this decade, including Undertone from earlier this year and 2024’s Civil War. It’s a big get for the studio and V/H/S as a whole: since 2021, the films have released on Shudder, including this year’s Mixtape movie. The second and third V/H/S film had limited theatrical runs and made tens of thousands during that time, while the original film made $1.9 million. That was in 2012, though, and in that time, horror’s become a much bigger genre that can have some long legs. Given SCP is a collaborative sci-fi/horror project that’s been going on since 2008, the movie can be an easy entry point to theatregoers. It’s surprising, then, to hear the actual SCP Foundation doesn’t actually have anything to do with the film. In a statement to AVClub, the Foundation explained its people tried reaching out to the A24, the filmmakers, and producers, and never got a reply back. What’s more, it said Deadline’s “incorrect” in A24 having worldwide rights, citing terms from the wiki’s Creative Commons ShareAlike license that allows the entire enterprise to exist. Under the license, derivative projects made using the SCP name have to abide by ShareAlike’s rules. Specifically, for this movie to fit within those parameters, the studio would have release it DRM-free and without “any sort of exclusivity with respect to distribution,” aka on YouTube and other streaming platforms at no cost, without taking legal action. The SCP Foundation called out the V/H/S: SCP filmmakers for “having no interest in engaging with the authors or curators of the material they’re adapting.” Nonetheless, it’s open to sitting down and discussing what can be properly done to make the film comply with its license. Given the movie’s vague 2027 release window, there’s plenty of time for more developments and information on the situation to emerge. Want more io9 news? item.title: In the Wild West of AI, Everybody Is Accusing Everybody Else of Theft
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.93
The AI boom has been fueled by the idea that all data is fair game, potential fodder for the training of new models. Little wonder then that ownership and intellectual property theft have become such sticky issues within the tech industry. On Thursday, Chinese robotics startup JoyIn—developer of a model called Aether—accused OpenAI of distilling its AI systems and stealing its website’s cosmic design aesthetic for the launch and branding of GPT-6 Astra. In an open letter written in Chinese, JoyIn CEO Guo Renjie said his company had started the process of filing a lawsuit, according to a translation from CNBC. (Gizmodo has not independently verified the report.) Distillation is a common industry practice in which developers use a larger, more advanced model as a sort of “teacher” to help train a smaller “student” model. But it’s become a controversial subject in recent months, as major American AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have repeatedly claimed that competitors in China have been using their proprietary models to conduct large-scale, illicit distillation efforts in order to gain a competitive edge. In a statement published Tuesday, the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said that some of the biggest Chinese AI firms—DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.ai—“are conducting systematic extraction of proprietary functionalities and capabilities of U.S. AI companies’ models through industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns that form the core—not merely a supplement—of their AI development strategy.” All this was likely being carried out with the knowledge and blessing of the Chinese government, according to CISA. Anthropic also said in a Thursday report that Moonshot, developer of an AI model called Kimi, had been carrying out a mechanical Turk-style trick to make its customers think they were getting responses from Kimi, when in fact they’d been generated by Claude. Guo’s letter to OpenAI is the first known case of a Chinese developer accusing an American company of distillation. It’s far from the first time that OpenAI has been accused of theft, though. The company has had to fend off a litany of lawsuits since the launch of ChatGPT a little under four years ago, filed by artists and news publishers arguing that their copyrighted work was used illegally to train new AI models. (OpenAI has repeatedly defended itself by invoking the so-called “fair use” standard of U.S. copyright law.) In July, Apple sued the company, claiming it had stolen company secrets in order to get its newborn hardware business off the ground. (Again, OpenAI has denied any wrongdoing.) Earlier this week, a NYU mathematics professor questioned whether his work on Codex had been surreptitiously used to train the model that OpenAI used to solve the Navier-Stokes “Millennium Problem.” (OpenAI told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation it “can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training.”) The irony of AI companies calling foul on “illicit” distillation when much of their business model depends on the nonconsensual scraping of online content seems to be lost on OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are preparing for what are expected to be record-breaking IPOs. At least for the time being, the line between “fair use” and theft within the unregulated AI industry is as hazy as the inner-workings of models themselves.

item.title: Three Batman Movies Return to Theaters Next Week
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.64
Warner Bros. and DC have made Batman Day a September staple for a decade, and for 2026, the occasion means a trip to the movies. For Saturday, September 19 and Sunday, September 20, theatregoers can see Tim Burton’s Batman or the animated flicks Mask of the Phantasm or The Lego Batman Movie on the big screen again. The 1989 movie was back in theaters for its 35th anniversary in 2024, while Mask and Lego have only had their initial theatrical runs. Of the three, the 1989 movie is the highest-grossing ($411.6 million worldwide), followed by Lego ($312 million) and Phantasm ($5.8 million). Beyond money, each of the Batman movies are significant in some fashion. Burton’s movie kickstarted the character’s modern dominance, while Lego’s re-release is nicely timed, given the Legacy of the Dark Knight game from earlier this year. Meanwhile, Mask of the Phantasm wasn’t just the first movie of the DCAU—which Batman: The Animated Series helped kick off—it’s also the only of those films to get a theatrical release. If there’s anything else planned for Batman Day, like a look at The Batman Part II or something for next month’s Clayface, Warner Bros. is keeping that under wraps. Even if there’s not, three pretty good movies covering different parts of the character’s history is good on its own, especially if you were too young or weren’t alive to see these on the big screen when they first came out. item.title: Altman Says OpenAI Won’t IPO This Year
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.18
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman just admitted that the company’s long-awaited, potentially record-setting IPO won’t be happening this year. Instead of rumored financial woes, Altman is blaming AI safety concerns for the timeline shift. “I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, this would right now be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman said in an interview with Fortune published over the weekend. OpenAI filed confidentially for an IPO earlier this summer, just days after competitor Anthropic it them to the punch. Although the company never shared a timeline on when the IPO would officially hit the market, for months now various media reports had been pencilling it in for this year, despite alleged disagreements between company executives on OpenAI’s financial readiness for an IPO. But now, Altman is saying not to expect the market debut until at least next year. That’s because there is “a lot of stuff to do” on the safety and alignment side of AI, Altman said, all of which he’d rather tackle as a private company. Artificial intelligence development has long been controversial, but over the past year the leading AI companies have faced increased public scrutiny over the safety of their models, especially with the recent introduction of models that the AI giants themselves deem potential cyber safety hazards. Those fears began with Anthropic’s Mythos model back in March and then crescendoed in July when OpenAI agents went rogue and hacked Hugging Face. What ensued were industry-wide pleas directed at the general public and regulatory bodies to take this rapid advance seriously and be worried about potentially catastrophic events once models reach AGI, a hypothetical and contested stage of AI in which it would outperform humans across all tasks. The AI industry’s plea is rather ironic considering that it’s the companies themselves that are developing these models and spearheading the advancements, and that the company executives are more than happy to lend their support to the Trump administration’s efforts to push for less global regulatory oversight. Meanwhile, some OpenAI executives are claiming that the company’s upcoming model has reached AGI-level capabilities. “We need to be able to make decisions that are not obviously in the interest of our business and our shareholders, for the responsibility of fulfilling our mission and what that’s going to require,” Altman told Fortune. “I think people should be happy that we are able and willing to not just like race ahead.” Part of that will require pausing more often during new model development to focus instead on improving safety and alignment, the OpenAI chief said, echoing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s sentiment to pace frontier AI development. In an essay published on Saturday, Amodei suggested that the industry “slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” so that “risk prevention has time to keep up.” In a very rare show of unison, both OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk took to X to voice their agreement with competitor Amodei. It’s also important to note that this joint awareness-raising effort bordering on doomerism comes as the AI industry contends with a major self-inflicted PR crisis. The general public has grown dramatically anti-AI within the last few months and critics are accusing AI developers of prioritizing profit over people and putting society at risk, citing the technology’s anticipated negative impact on everything from the labor market to the environment. “If you’re like ‘Oh, OpenAI is not going to pause because they’re worried about it costing their business money,’ you like very deeply misunderstand us,” Altman claimed in the interview. But those fears are not completely unsubstantiated. Just under a year ago, OpenAI found itself in major trouble after its sycophantic ChatGPT model GPT-4o was tied to several severe and fatal mental health episodes in frequent users. A New York Times report from late last year suggested that company leadership was aware of the problem with GPT-4o, but ultimately decided to release the model anyway. Another report, this time published by The New Yorker earlier this year, characterized Altman as untrustworthy, claiming that the CEO had lied to the OpenAI board about the safety testing of GPT-4, the model preceding GPT-4o.

item.title: Your mesh Wi-Fi's backhaul is destroying your NAS performance
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.11
If you've ever used a mesh Wi-Fi system, you've probably noticed that the satellite nodes usually have a spare Ethernet port. It is tempting to use that port to attach a NAS. After all, it seems like a good way to get your NAS connected without running a cable across the floor or through a wall. However, that port isn't really well-suited for use with a NAS. The wireless back haul may not be up to a NAS's demands Back haul may not have enough bandwidth available Wireless Wi-Fi nodes work using a second "back haul" connection. It is a special connection (usually Wi-Fi-based) that links the satellite node to your main router. So, even though your NAS is physically plugged into a node with a cable, the data it sends and receives instantly gets transmitted over the Wi-Fi to the main router anyway. It has all the same limitations and problems as a regular Wi-Fi network, like interference from other devices or physical obstructions. If you're backing up or streaming 4K media or a huge photo archive, you're almost certainly going to notice a bottleneck caused by whatever connection limitations the back haul network has. In most scenarios, you're better off just directly connecting your NAS to the Wi-Fi directly if your NAS supports that. At least then you have greater discretion over where you place it. Not all NAS units have Wi-Fi, and only some support Wi-Fi dongles. Wired is more stable Your wireless throughput is less stable than a wired connection Many consumer NAS units today have gigabit, 2.5 gigabit, or even 5 gigabit Ethernet ports. On a wired network, you can expect even Cat6 to hit those speeds easily over residential distances, and it'll likely be very stable too. With a wireless back haul on a budget mesh system, the situation is almost certainly going to be worse. Even if you see decent speeds, which I'd consider anything about 50 megabytes per second, those numbers are going to fluctuate depending on all sorts of external factors. In the times I've used a wireless back haul, I found that other devices on the back haul often caused pretty significant performance hits, and it isn't anything weird either. Even someone streaming video on their phone can be enough to impact the performance of wireless back hauls. That doesn't even begin to address other issues that may arise if you live in a crowded Wi-Fi environment, like an apartment building. Your NAS needs to be online almost 100% of the time Back haul drops and node reboots take the NAS offline A NAS needs to be online as much as possible. If it disconnects at an inopportune time, it can abort a massive backup mid-run, corrupt an open database, or leave your mapped network drives in a "broken" state until you manually reconnect. Unfortunately, mesh satellites are inherently a little volatile. Even if you don't mind the speed variability, satellites are prone to reconnecting, can sometimes automatically optimize their channels, or reboot for a firmware update. Every time one of those events happens, the NAS you have connected to the device will be offline. Unfortunately, automatic updates often roll out overnight—the exact same time that people schedule their backups. On more than one occasion, I had an automated backup fail when a mesh node was temporarily disrupted overnight. After that, I drilled some holes in the walls and ran an Ethernet cable directly to my router. Of course, your main router needs to reboot occasionally too, but that is still less common than an interruption caused by connectivity or renegotiation. Similarly, wired switches are usually extremely simple—many don't need updates and don't need to reboot. So long as the wire remains connected and undamaged, they'll run for years without interruption. If you have the option, try to ensure that your Wi-Fi system doesn't perform automated updates during your backup windows. Keep your NAS near your router if possible If you're just trying to connect something like a printer, the Ethernet port on a mesh node is fine. However, your NAS should really be connected via an Ethernet cable directly to your router. The best choice is to directly plug your NAS into your router's LAN port. If that isn't an option, attach it to a simple wired switch connected to your router instead. It is also a good idea to keep both devices attached to the same UPS if you have one—it ensures that your devices will usually both be online at the same time, and neither device is likely to try to reach the other while it is offline. If the NAS can't sit directly next to your router, run an Ethernet cable or use a MoCA (which allows internet over coax cable) instead. MoCA introduces some hiccups, but I've found it is more reliable across longer distances than most ISP-supplied mesh Wi-Fi systems are. And, finally, if the NAS cannot be wired to the router directly and your NAS has Wi-Fi functionality, just place it in the same room as the router. The Wi-Fi connection will be much more reliable than the back haul from a node.

item.title: This open-source Windows launcher does what Microsoft’s new Start menu should have done
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.29
After years of complaints about how little you could customize the Windows Start menu, Microsoft is finally overhauling it in the 26H2 update. In reality, though, they are only catching up to something an open-source app figured out years ago. Meet Flow Launcher, a keyboard-first app launcher that is superior to the current Start menu from all directions. Trying Flow Launcher for the first time The productivity boost felt like cheating To test this praised tool out myself, I went straight to the official Flow Launcher website to grab a copy. There were multiple download options, including a portable version, an EXE file, and also through package managers such as WinGet. I went for the portable version for a quick setup. Though that meant I had to create a shortcut myself. The setup process was intuitive, as the onboarding pages took you through some of the essential things you should know about the launcher, including shortcut keys, hotkeys, and explaining action keywords. On first launch, I'm welcomed by a search bar, followed by a list of commands. The UI looked nice and blended well with Windows 11. I also noticed a clicky sound every time I opened it with Alt+Space. The most common functionality for the launcher is searching, especially searching for and launching apps. I like to pin apps I use often to my Taskbar and the Start menu. However, that means I have to use the mouse to click the app to open it. With Flow Launcher, I only had to start typing its name and hit Enter. But that's not all. Searching for an app is blazing fast. By the time you finish typing the name halfway, the result is already there. It's not just apps, though. You can also search for files and open them in the default file opener. This is much more useful as I don't have to remember where I kept that one pesky file or use Windows File Explorer's slow search. As long as I remember the name, that's enough. If Windows search drives you crazy, this could be a lifesaver. Flow Launcher itself is highly customizable You'll get lost playing around its settings Talking about customizing the customizer. You can tweak General and Appearance settings. Let's explore both. The General settings tab contains the settings that shape the behavior and functionality of the launcher. For example, whether or not you want to start Flow Launcher on system startup, hide its tray icon, whether it should be on top of other windows, and more. One setting I liked a lot is Always Preview. It opens a new panel on the side that shows the icon of the searched app and some details. Not only does it enhance the overall look of the app, but it's also helpful when you need some quick details about the app or file. The Appearance tab is all about the look and feel. There are almost 20 themes to choose from. Mine was set to Windows 11 by default, which explains why it looked like a native app. I went with the Rider theme, which looked more polished to me. Other things you can customize are animation, sound effects, icons, badges, window size, and the color scheme, among others. If you turned on Always Preview, some of the results may not take effect since the preview panel takes up some space in the full launcher window. You can also adjust the clock and date here. I found that turning on both squishes them together, with no space in between. So I turned off the date. The plugin ecosystem is where it really pulls ahead Turning a launcher into a control center In the settings, you'll find a Plugins and a Plugin Store section. The Plugins section contains plugins you've already installed in Flow Launcher. The store has more you can try. And this is really where things turn more interesting as you keep extending what the launcher can do. In the Plugins section, you can turn a plugin on or off. Each plugin also has a dropdown menu that contains some settings regarding it. For example, the Browser Bookmarks plugin lets you choose the browser(s) you want to load from. Each plugin lets you set an action keyword for it. The Plugin Store was quite amusing to explore. There is an ocean of plugins to be installed in a wide range of categories, from productivity and study to gaming and development. You can search, update, and install plugins. You can also choose a plugin from your local path. Installing a plugin is also straightforward. You click on the plugin and click Install. Once installed, you'll need to restart Flow Launcher to use it. Some of the plugins I found useful are Speed Test, File Folder Opener, Google Translate, and some of the math plugins. One thing I wish is that each plugin had a dedicated page where I could check the details of the plugins. You can see them by clicking a link that opens the GitHub page of the plugin. However, having a page inside the Plugin Store would be much more intuitive. Microsoft still has some catching up to do While PowerToys Run and Command Palette have quite similar functions and capabilities, the Start menu still feels left behind. Moreover, Flow Launcher has an upper hand over the PowerToys tools if you love customization and you want to become a power user.

item.title: I stopped using Word for simple notes after discovering this ridiculously capable text editor
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.35
Most of us learned Microsoft Word while growing up and never really questioned it. It was on most computers, so it became the default for everything, including notes that had no business being formatted like a printed document. You don't need an entire document to take a few notes; you should use an app built to manage them like databases. Word was built for printing, not real note-taking Notion treats your notes like data Microsoft Word is the go-to app for everyone. It's not hard to see why, because it's kind of built into so many of our childhoods. I was taught Word in elementary school, and Microsoft Office tended to be used in plenty of classrooms. However, it was never designed for quick, messy notes. It was built to make print-ready documents. The whole architecture is print-first, which means everything is built around wrapping text onto physical pages like A4 or Letter. That makes a ton of formatting overhead when you're just trying to write information in real time, so structuring text tends not to be the most important thing. The file system model doesn't help either. Documents live in folders, links break if you move or rename anything, and a note can only be in one folder at a time. Syncing across devices is its own issue that I don't even bother with anymore due to the bugs. Since Word is constantly doing layout calculations in the background because of things like page breaks and floating images, it's really bad at spatial organization and handling more complex additions to documents. I like the apps that treat the page like a page, and not like paper. One that does this well is Notion, because it treats your pages like a database. The workspace becomes a graph of linked blocks, and there's no real difference between a string of text, an image, a checklist, a database row, or a whole page. Every block is atomic, and you can move, nest, or transform things without losing data. So indenting a block changes the database render tree, not just the visual styling. Synced blocks solve the duplication problem too. A single block can exist on multiple pages, and edits can spread everywhere. It overall makes your life easier. Notion is built around little blocks instead of normal pages The block system makes writing a lot easier So Notion's whole workspace is a lot more complicated than it seems, but it makes a lot of sense when you get used to it. It's built around this editor, except instead of a normal document that just goes top to bottom, everything is a structured tree of little modular pieces that live on their own. Hitting Tab actually changes the underlying database relationships and moves that block's ID into the children list of the block above it. Since the data is decoupled from the style, everything survives type changes. Basically, if you have a checked to-do item and turn it into a heading, the rendering engine just ignores the checked flag. But the flag is still stored. If you turn it back into a to-do later, then the checkmark will come right back, because the metadata was never thrown away. For actually taking notes day to day, I've found that slash commands make things easier than Word does. You type /and a searchable menu pops up, so you don't have to grab the mouse and dig through toolbars. Start typing, and it filters in real time. /todo gives you a checkbox, /table drops in a grid, /toggle makes a collapsible section. There are also ones like /duplicate or /comment, and you can even do visual highlights like /red or /blue backgrounds without stopping your typing. While there are arguments as to why Microsoft Word doesn't make things this easy, it feels like these are the kinds of changes the company should push for. Instead, we have Copilot being forced into way too many apps. Notion has its fair share of problems You trade raw speed for way better organization Notion can be kind of annoying. It's cloud-dependent and runs on a huge JavaScript stack, so it's just not as fast as a blank Word document. The desktop app is built on Electron and React, which means it has to load a massive framework before you can even type. My computer is older, so it takes around five to ten seconds. Word opens in under a second because it's a native app, but even the online version loads incredibly quickly. It also takes a bit of time to learn Notion. I was initially turned off by it because it felt like I was setting up a Wikipedia page instead of taking notes. However, that tiny bit of lag and setup you get with Notion is a pretty small price for having everything you write easy to find and all connected in one system. That said, Word isn't going anywhere. Even with all the new AI features getting built in, it's still the standard. So if you genuinely like a notepad that feels like it was built for a printer, use Word. However, if you want to feel like your notes have a lot more depth and control, try out Notion. Notion is not an easy switch from Word Notion isn't a clean swap for Word, but that's a good thing in some ways. The learning curve is the hardest part to get through, but once you know how to use Notion, it's a lot of fun to pair with AI and other things. I use Antigravity to help organize the random notes I have, and it works like a charm. The setup cost is a few hours, and what you get at the end is a really good app. Notion - OS - Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and web browsers - Supported Desktop Browsers - Web Clipper Extension for Chrome, Firefox, Safari This customizable workspace simplifies and combines the processes of note-taking, task creation, and date planning to create an all-in-one productivity workspace.

item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 6.47
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.31
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: Ray-Ban Meta glasses update makes them more useful on the go
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.72
What you need to know - Meta AI glasses v28 update adds pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, expanded language support, and camera anti-tampering improvements. - With hands-free walking directions, you can ask Meta to navigate to nearby destinations, with driving directions sent to your phone for farther trips. - Spatial Audio makes listening richer and adds a more immersive layer to music and podcasts on supported Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Meta has been steadily expanding what its AI glasses can do, and the latest v28 update adds several practical upgrades, including pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, and broader language support. Perhaps the headline addition is pedestrian navigation. You can now ask the smart glasses to guide you on foot to nearby destinations using voice commands such as “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” If you’re farther away, the glasses can send driving directions to your phone. There’s also a new way to begin navigation from your phone: Find a destination in your mapping app, tap Share, and select Meta AI, and navigation will start on your connected glasses. The update also broadens where walking directions work. Meta says it now offers walking directions in the U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, and some cities across the world. Audio gets an upgrade as well. Now, Spatial Audio can make a more immersive version of the stereo sound you’re already getting, whether that’s music or a podcast. You can find this option in Settings > Audio > Spatial. It works with Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Optics and the Meta Glasses collection. Meta is also adding Mandarin Chinese (zh_CN) support across Device Controls, calls and messaging, media capture and music controls, Meta AI, and MMAI. Finally, v28 has ongoing anti-tampering improvements to protect the cameras on the glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Earlier firmware releases introduced features like Conversation Focus, which uses the microphones in the glasses to help users hear nearby voices better, and deeper Spotify integration. Similarly, on Reddit, the response is pragmatic, with users mostly praising the glasses for hands-free photos, calls, podcasts, and open-ear audio, while battery life and Meta AI’s limitations remain common complaints. item.title: Arm's upcoming GPU for Android claims it can deliver 'desktop-class' graphics—I hope it's true
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.34
What you need to know - Arm revealed the work put into empowering its new Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, which is said to bring "desktop-class" graphics to phones. - Arm states it's leaning on an AI-native Mali GPU with a Neural Accelerator and more to handle demanding graphics, while maintaining smooth frame rates for mobile gamers. - Qualcomm also teased its upcoming Adreno GPU for the next Snapdragon chips, stating it will also lean on AI to help with graphics rendering and frame rate generation. Arm is highlighting what mobile users can expect from its next GPU. It states everything it's worked to implement is due to growing user demands for "richer visuals" and better frame rates. Arm revealed the Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU in a newsroom post this week. According to its data, Arm says mobile users want a few things: "They want richer visuals, smoother frame rates, and increasingly immersive experiences." However, there are certain challenges it reportedly needs to overcome to help consumers (and developers, too). The Mali G2-Ultra NX is purportedly the answer to everyone's problems. Arm states it built the GPU for "neural graphics." This is an AI-native Mali GPU—its first-ever—which brings the Neural Accelerator into shader cores. This reportedly aids better teamwork between the graphics and computing workloads. What's more, performance is said to increase. Arm states its Neural Accelerator helps the GPU "handle increasingly demanding scenes more efficiently." This would give developers creating more pleasing visuals more room without the cost of reduced frame rates. Arm's third-generation ray tracing technology will also assist the graphics department. The Mali G2-Ultra NX support for this ray tracing software will facilitate advancements in shadows, complex lighting, reflections, and more. At a hardware level, Arm states devices with Opacity Micromaps support can produce "richer foliage, more detailed fabrics, layered surfaces, and more." Better graphics are nothing without smooth frame rates. Arm says "architectural improvements" in the GPU can support longer gaming sessions at "up to" 120FPS. AI comes to the aid of mobile graphics? We've been hearing about AI's involvement with mobile phone graphics since earlier this month. Qualcomm highlighted its Adreno "Neural Fusion" GPU, stating that it will lean on AI to upgrade mobile gaming graphics. The chip reportedly utilizes AI-driven rendering tech. This new tech will put better gaming resolution and frame generation in the graphics pipeline. Console-like graphics were a major detail for Qualcomm in that announcement. The company claims its new chip, coupled with AI, will reduce the work the chip needs to do to produce the graphics mobile users have been asking for. All of this is en route to the Dual 8 Elites from Qualcomm during the Snapdragon Summit from September 22-24. item.title: RIP Pixel Tablet: Google has officially pulled the plug
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.94
What you need to know - Google has officially removed the Pixel Tablet from its online store after listing it as out of stock. - The Pixel Tablet has also disappeared from major retailers including Amazon and Best Buy. - Google reportedly canceled plans for second- and third-generation Pixel Tablets due to sales and profitability concerns. - Existing Pixel Tablet owners will continue receiving software updates until mid-2028 despite the lineup's end. The Pixel Tablet is finally dead. Like, properly dead dead. Google launched the Pixel Tablet back in 2023 as a hybrid device that could work as both a traditional Android tablet and a smart home display when placed on its charging dock. At $499, the Pixel Tablet offered a pretty interesting combination on paper, but reactions to the device were mixed after launch. Google reportedly had plans for a second-generation Pixel Tablet in 2025 and even a third-generation model in 2027. But amid poor sales and profitability concerns, the company reportedly pulled the plug on those plans back in 2024. Despite that, the original Pixel Tablet remained available through the Google Store and retailers for quite some time. Until now. As spotted by Jetstream, Google has officially removed the Pixel Tablet from the Google Store. The tablet was listed as "out of stock" until a few days ago, but the product page has now been removed altogether, effectively confirming that Google is done selling the device. The Pixel Tablet has also disappeared from retailers, including Amazon and Best Buy. That means there's now no official way to buy a new Pixel Tablet. You may still be able to find remaining stock through smaller online retailers or pick one up from a reseller, but Google's own inventory is officially gone. The good news for existing Pixel Tablet owners is that software support isn't ending anytime soon. Google is expected to continue supporting the device with updates until mid-2028. But unless Google decides to resurrect its tablet ambitions again, there won't be another Pixel Tablet waiting to replace it. The Pixel Tablet was an interesting idea. Having one device that could work as both an Android tablet and a smart home display made plenty of sense, especially inside Google's ecosystem. Unfortunately, the idea never really took off. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android So, RIP Pixel Tablet. This time, it looks like it's actually over. Sanuj is a tech writer who loves exploring smartphones, tablets, and wearables. He began his journey with a Nokia Lumia and later dived deep into Android and iPhone. He's been writing about tech since 2018, with bylines at Pocketnow, Android Police, Pocket-Lint, and MakeUseOf. When he's not testing gadgets, he's either sipping chai, watching football, or playing cricket. item.title: Samsung is shutting down a couple of apps; vows to return new and improved
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.83
What you need to know - Samsung is alerting users about its preparations to shut down the Quick Measure and AR Doodle apps on December 31, 2026. - While Samsung acknowledges "inconveniences" from this, it states that it's "committed" to returning these apps "with improved services" in the future. - In July, Samsung officially axed its Messages app, which has been replaced by the Google Messages app. Samsung is preparing to shut down two apps, and it's delivering warnings to users in preparation for what's to come. Very early this morning (Sept 7), Tarun Vats on X noticed new warnings from Samsung about two apps that are being phased out. Samsung says that it will shut down the Quick Measure app on December 31, 2026. It adds, "After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it's already downloaded, but be aware that some features may not function properly." The Quick Measure app currently works with Google's Wear OS. However, after this termination date from Samsung, it says app support will no longer be provided for new Wear OS versions. Quick Measure isn't the only app getting the boot. Users replying to Vats' thread on X mentioned Samsung's AR Doodle is also getting axed come December 31. A similar warning to users was given for AR Doodle. The date remains the same; however, it swaps Wear OS for regular OS, as this app likely relies on Android/One UI updates. While Samsung recognizes that shutting down an app can cause "inconveniences," the news isn't all bad. Samsung says, "We are committed to returning with improved services in the future." It's not clear if Quick Measure and AR Doodle will return upgraded, new, and improved. Or if we'll see brand-new variations that change these older systems. Another app got shutdown this summer Not going to lie, I had to dig pretty far back to even find anything about Quick Measure. Not sure how many people are going to miss the feature, but I'm there are some out there. It's interesting, considering everything the Samsung Health app can do today. If Samsung is committed to returning in some revamped form, I wonder if these features would find new lives inside existing, supported apps, rather than standalone gigs. If you're confused about "Quick Measure," we wouldn't blame you. Our earliest coverage dates back to 2021, when Samsung rolled out new features for its S Health app (yeah... S Health). That update coincided with the company's Gear Fit 2 launch. Quick Measure let users check their heart rate without launching the full app. Our coverage read, "Simply activate Quick Measure, and you'll now be able to place a finger on the heart rate sensor and wait for a reading." We've come a long way with heart rate tracking and the like related to cardiovascular health. Anyway, the last app shutdown from Samsung was its Messages app in July. Google Messages was reported to be the company's official replacement for users to text. However, consumers with Android 11 and under "are unaffected, and emergency calls still work after the shutdown." item.title: Samsung might've started racing ahead to Android XR glasses with a color display
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.68
What you need to know - Rumors claim Samsung is developing a new pair of smart glasses, and has tapped Samsung Display for an in-lens color display. - The glasses would allegedly focus on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and more" on an extremely thin panel. - Samsung has its Intelligent Eyewear, which is supposedly coming out this fall, but those are mostly voice-focused with Google's Gemini and a camera. Samsung has barely dipped a toe into the world of smart glasses, and there's already a rumor that it wants to go bigger next time. This report from The Elec (Korean) claims Samsung might've started developing smart glasses with a color display (via 9to5Google). The publication cites its "industry sources" in saying Samsung has tapped Samsung Display to "create microdisplays" for a future pair of AI smart glasses. These rumors claim Samsung has a lot on its plate to prepare this product. Specifically, the post claims Samsung has a "technical challenge" to overcome: its FOV (field of view). The company is purportedly chasing a wide FOV for these glasses to accommodate the information users would see. What's more, Samsung is leaning on its Display side to create "ultra-small panels" of ~0.2 inches or smaller for the lenses. Samsung is allegedly focusing on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and navigation arrows" (machine-translated). It's still incredibly early to know for sure how Samsung's first color display smart glasses will arrive. However, the publication suggests the glasses could see a launch in the second half of 2027 or "early" in 2028. Got lenses? Samsung's getting serious. I don't think its Intelligent Eyewear are a bad start, though. It's starting simple. Useful, even. Everything is based on your voice. You still have a camera to take photos, and Gemini is there to help with hands-free assistance. To put a color display—a proper screen—would definitely take things up a notch. To me, I think this rumor is probably a little more eye-catching. We can't help but think about the Ray-Ban Display glasses from Meta. In fact, that's probably the kind of competition Samsung wants to get itself involved in. These glasses also feature the neural band. It makes it easier to control the display and content on your lenses with hand gestures. There's plenty of time still to see how Samsung manages this. Right now, we have (kind of) Samsung's "Intelligent Eyewear." These glasses are in partnership with Google, alongside designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. These are Samsung's first smart glasses, but they lean more on the user's voice. Users can communicate with Gemini for navigation, order pickups, and photos. The glasses feature a camera and a microphone to get all of this done. Google reiterated its Samsung partnership during this summer's Unpacked. These glasses aren't out yet. During the original announcement this past spring, Samsung said we shouldn't expect to see them until "later this fall." item.title: This new slim phone puts a 6,000mAh battery in a seriously thin frame
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.56
What you need to know - The TECNO Camon Slim 5G is here, and it's just 6.39mm thick while packing a hefty 6,000mAh battery. - It features a curved "swan-neck" profile and five distinct finishes, including photochromic technology on the Neo Mondrian variant and a swirling Starry Night gradient on Van Gogh Blue. - Despite its slim profile, it boasts MIL-STD-810 drop resistance, IP69K/IP69/IP68/IP66 water/dust ratings, and wet-hand touch functionality. TECNO appears to be pretty serious about the whole “slim phone” thing. Its latest phone, the Camon Slim 5G, is a mere 6.39mm thin but packs a 6,000mAh battery, a 50MP Sony camera, and a number of AI features into its compact body. The device also places a lot of emphasis on design. The Camon 50 series’ curved “swan-neck” profile is carried over from the Camon 50 series, but five finishes give the phone very different personalities: Burgundy Red, Neo Mondrian, Matisse Black, Van Gogh Blue, and Rebel Pink. Some of those finishes are very interesting. Neo Mondrian uses photochromic technology to show colorful geometric blocks on UV light, while Van Gogh Blue has a patterned gradient coating to create a swirling effect based on The Starry Night. Matisse Black adds fluorescent green accents to a black fiberglass body, while Burgundy Red and Rebel Pink are a more traditional take on the artistic theme. On the optics side, the 50MP Sony LYTIA 700C main camera features a 1/1.56-inch sensor, close-loop autofocus, and a triple stabilization system of OIS, EIS, and AI Shutter. TECNO’s Super-Zoom FlashSnap can automatically capture fast-moving moments with shutter speeds of up to 1/11236 seconds and 2x telephoto shooting. You also get 24mm, 35mm, and 50mm portrait options supported by TECNO Universal Tone for skin-tone rendering. The optional Mag Badge adds a 1.73-inch AMOLED screen, remote shutter control up to 10 meters away, and selfie previews. The AI toolkit is more than photo editing. The AI Snap Poster makes product graphics, AI Recording Notes turns lectures into organized notes, AI Class Schedule digitizes class schedules, and AI Healthy Eating calculates calories and nutrients from food images. Again, thinness does not mean TECNO has ignored durability. IP69K/IP69/IP68/IP66 protection, MIL-STD-810 certification, and wet-touch features ensure the phone is protected from the elements. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The 6.78-inch 1.5K 144Hz AMOLED panel is capable of dealing with rain and even use through a waterproof case. It runs on the Dimensity 7300e 5G chip under the hood, with three major OS upgrades and five years of security updates promised. The Camon Slim 5G is being rolled out in different markets, but TECNO has not yet announced local pricing. Selected markets will also get a three-month trial of Google AI Plus with 2TB storage. item.title: Moto wants in: a wide Razr foldable just had its design leaked
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.50
What you need to know - A major leak claims Motorola is developing a wide Razr Fold to compete with Samsung, Huawei, and more. - The device could fit that small, passport-like design with an "easy-open" profile," a "bezel-less" cover display, and a dual lens horizontal camera bar. - An anonymous source claims the phone could debut "in the coming months." Wide foldables are quickly becoming a popular trend. Leaks from over the weekend claim Motorola could be the next brand to hop on that train. Leaks revealed by Android Headlines, courtesy of an "anonymous source," suggest the design Motorola is going for. Its source allegedly provided a few sketches, which purportedly showcase the various design ideas for the wide Razr foldable. One thing rumors claim is that Motorola's foldable could feature an "easy-open" profile. Among theories of a crease-less display and "3D glass," the wide Razr foldable's frame "isn't flat." The report states this decision could help make the device easier for consumers to open on the fly. This wide Razr Fold certainly fits the bill in these leaked illustrations. Offering that shorter (perhaps even stout) frame with rounded corners. "Motorola" will allegedly be inscribed on the hinge, visible when folded. Curiously, one illustration, depicting the phone's cover display, suggests it could be "bezel-less." What's more, the device could feature a horizontal, protruding camera bar, similar to Google's Pixels. Its camera array hasn't been narrowed down, but there's speculation that it might offer dual lenses. Android Headlines was reportedly told by the anonymous source that Motorola is preparing to launch this "Wide Razr Fold" (or whatever it'll be called) "in the coming months." Moto's going wide If anything, Moto's wide Razr Fold might feel closer to what Huawei did with the Pura V Max. The company's "horizontally wide" foldable featured that landscape camera bar. The device feels more like a passport, which Google has done with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold and Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. Huawei's wide foldable this year features a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.5-inch cover screen. The current Moto rumors had nothing to say on this front, so we'll have to wait a while. The idea of a wider foldable is something more and more people have become curious about. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 was incredibly popular for Samsung after a week of pre-orders. Consumers overseas crashed websites with their early orders 30 minutes after the phone went live. Shipping dates were also pushed back, since Samsung needed to manufacture more phones to meet demand. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Android Central's Take Motorola got in on the "regular" fold (Moto Razr Fold) aesthetic earlier this year, and the phone looks pretty good. In fact, one of my colleagues said in their review that the phone gives Samsung a new reason to worry. Motorola made some good moves, but it's clear it wants to continue. Hopping on the wide-fold train is the next "best thing." We'll just have to see when/if the phone arrives. These sketches look nice, but they aren't enough for me yet.
