item.title: Powering AI is an architecture problem
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.39
Sponsored Provided byON.energy On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world's largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of load off the grid in seconds. And it wasn't the first time. Two years earlier, a single failed surge arrester dropped roughly 60 Virginia facilities and 1,500 megawatts at once. No one could anticipate so much uniform load responding to grid faults the same way, at the same time. The AI power debate is mostly about generation: more turbines, more solar, more transmission. The grid needs more electrons. But the outages in Virginia weren't supply failures; they were architecture failures. And a giant wave of interconnections is arriving on that same architecture, putting grid reliability at risk. It's a problem nobody wants to own. Asking more from the grid The grid was built around predictable loads: steel mills, refineries, and houses at dinnertime. Different load sizes, same process—drawing power smoothly, misbehaving occasionally, and recovering gracefully. But AI data centers don't behave that way. An AI campus can swing 70% of its load in milliseconds during a training run, then trip offline just as fast at the first sign of trouble upstream to protect billions in compute. Each is rational alone. Together, at gigawatt scale, they're a problem the grid has never solved—and the next wave of data center campuses is planned at exactly that scale. Where the old stack breaks The standard data center power stack hasn't changed in decades. Medium-voltage power arrives, transformers step it down, low-voltage uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units condition it, and it reaches the racks. Push that design to AI scale, and it cracks in three places. First, the UPS sits deep inside the building, close to the racks. But its batteries are an undersized spare tire, designed to handle an outage for a few minutes, not to absorb load swings this fast and volatile around the clock. Second, the UPS spends most of its life in bypass. Legacy converters waste enough power that operators run in eco-mode: A static switch feeds the racks directly from the grid and nothing filters in either direction. The compute's swings go out raw, and grid transients—sub-millisecond events that can damage or take down equipment—come in too fast for any switch to catch. Third, the protection logic was written when "large load" meant 50 megawatts. This protection logic can't see the grid it is now a part of, so when trouble hits upstream, it does exactly the wrong thing: it drops out. In the 2024 Virginia event, most of the lost load traced to protection schemes that count voltage dips and disconnect on the third one—as designed, at the worst moment. This isn't sloppy engineering. It's careful engineering the load has outgrown. Moving into the path The fix is three moves, made together. Move it up—from 480 volts to medium voltage (13.8 kilovolts and higher), the voltage large sites draw from the grid. Move it out—from the data hall to modular enclosures near the substation so the building holds only compute and the cooling that keeps it alive. Move it into the path—instead of a battery that watches and reacts, a system every electron runs through, all the time. There's nothing to detect and nothing to switch because nothing was ever routed around it. On paper, three straightforward upgrades. In practice, they rewrite every line item downstream. Making the change When thousands of GPUs spin up together, the system absorbs the swing and hands the grid a flat load profile. When a disturbance hits, the equipment behind it never notices. A difficult neighbor becomes a predictable one. And when the utility needs help, it becomes a useful one. Interconnection changes, too. The utility certifies one medium-voltage box instead of untangling every transformer, UPS, chiller, pump, and switchgear lineup behind it. Engineers swap chip generations without a fresh interconnection study. Months come off the permitting timeline. Inside the fence, UPS rooms become compute or cooling space. Density per construction dollar climbs. And the economics flip. Equipment that runs at medium voltage, sits outside, and stores its own energy can qualify for tax credits, and earn revenue in grid programs like peak shaving and demand response. Backup power stops being insurance and starts paying for itself. The architecture test In early 2026, we tested a full-scale system at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a U.S. Department of Energy facility and the only place in the Western Hemisphere that can replicate real grid faults and AI-scale load swings concurrently in the same loop. We hit it from both directions: real AI load profiles hit the compute side at full medium voltage. Grid faults hit the utility side, including a full zero-voltage event. The compute side didn't flinch. Neither did the grid side. It cleared the large-load voltage ride-through requirements from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the grid operator, with room to spare. Those rules exist because operators no longer take facilities this size on faith, and more are coming. Most of the industry treats them as hurdles. A medium-voltage, inline system clears them out of the box. Compliance isn't an added feature. It's what the architecture does. The new layer Much of what looks like a grid problem in the AI buildout sits inside the fence, in equipment sized for a load that no longer exists. Move the right pieces up, out, and into the path, and a grid liability becomes a grid asset. Density goes up. Permitting time comes down. Backup power earns its keep. The engineering works—and the next wave of AI factories is being built on it. The industry hasn't named this layer yet. We call it the medium-voltage AI UPS. The name matters less than the choice: those factories can arrive as a strain on the grid or as strength for it. We already know how to build the second kind. This content was produced by ON.energy. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: Healthcare AI’s next test is integration
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.33
Sponsored Provided byEnsemble The entrance of major AI companies into healthcare is a meaningful and welcome development, accelerating the technical foundation available to the industry. Their models are increasingly capable of processing long clinical records, interpreting complex terminology, comparing documentation against evidence and generating coherent summaries from large volumes of information. For clinicians, operators, and administrative teams who spend significant time searching through fragmented data, these advances are helping reduce cognitive burden and make high-value information easier to access. But healthcare leaders should not confuse model capability with operational capability. Healthcare’s administrative challenges are caused by fragmented information, fragmented workflows, and fragmented accountability, not a lack of information. The industry has spent decades investing in systems that capture activity: electronic health records, billing platforms, payer portals, scheduling systems, call center platforms, and analytics applications. Each system records something important. But few were designed to reason across the full chain of decisions that determines whether patients get timely access, clinicians have the right documentation and providers are reimbursed appropriately. This is the problem that AI must now confront. Revenue cycle is becoming one of healthcare AI’s proving grounds The revenue cycle is the process healthcare providers use to get paid for care — from scheduling and registration through coding, billing, payer follow-up, and payment collection. It is unusually suited to rigorous AI deployment because it combines high transaction volume, complex reasoning, structured and unstructured data, measurable outcomes, and significant operational variation. It also sits at the intersection of financial performance, patient access, and administrative workload. A single claim can be influenced by patient insurance information, clinical documentation, coding rules, payer-specific policies, prior authorization requirements, medical necessity criteria, and many other data sources and operational processes. A breakdown in any one of those areas can create downstream consequences weeks or months later. This is why generic automation has often fallen short. Traditional robotic process automation works well when workflows are stable and rules are predictable, but healthcare administration is neither. Payer requirements change. Documentation expectations evolve. Exceptions are common and often material. Large language models improve part of the equation, extracting meaning from narrative text, summarizing records and supporting reasoning over complex documentation. But when used alone, they inherit important limitations. They may produce plausible outputs without sufficient traceability. They may lack awareness of local workflow constraints. They may miss payer-specific history or context that determines whether an action is likely to change an outcome. Why foundation models will become necessary but insufficient The major AI firms are solving real technical problems for healthcare. Better context windows make it easier to process longitudinal records. Stronger reasoning improves the interpretation of complex clinical scenarios. Better multimodal capabilities may eventually help connect text, imaging, structured data, and clinical signals in more useful ways. Safer model behavior and healthcare-specific tuning will continue to improve adoption. These capabilities will make healthcare work faster, more consistent and easier to navigate. But they will not, on their own, solve deep-rooted administrative complexity. Much of healthcare’s operational knowledge does not live in general medical literature, coding manuals, or public payer guidance. It lives in the accumulated experience of what actually happens after decisions are made. For example: - Why does one appeal strategy outperform another? - Which documentation gaps are most likely to cause reimbursement delay? - How does a specific payer respond to a particular clinical argument? These insights are behavioral, operational, and longitudinal. They emerge from years of transactions, outcomes, exceptions, and human judgment. As foundation models become more capable, access to baseline healthcare knowledge will become less differentiating. Most leading systems will be able to interpret ICD-10 codes, recognize medical terminology, summarize payer policies, and reason over public clinical criteria. The durable advantage will come from how organizations combine that model intelligence with proprietary operational data, structured knowledge, workflow context, and governance. The technical shift: From automation to orchestration Agentic orchestration turns foundation model understanding into coordinated action — intelligence that can follow work across systems, apply the right rules, adapt when something changes, and keep learning from what happens next. A prior authorization workflow, for example, may require retrieving clinical documentation through fast healthcare interoperability resources (FHIR) APIs, mapping patient history to payer criteria, identifying missing evidence, generating a submission packet, routing exceptions to a specialist, monitoring payer response, adjusting patient care pathways, and learning from the outcome. This type of workflow requires coordination. It also requires guardrails: regulatory requirements, privacy standards, clinical policies, coding rules, payer criteria, and organizational risk thresholds. One promising approach is hybrid architecture that combines LLMs with structured knowledge bases, symbolic logic, reinforcement learning, and deterministic validation layers. At Ensemble, this is the design principle behind EIQ, our revenue cycle intelligence engine. EIQ brings together operational activity, clinical documentation, payer behavior, and reimbursement outcomes into a continuously learning intelligence layer that’s integrated with the hospital’s electronic health record (EHR). It supplements the system of record with a system of intelligence, designed to connect information and surface actions most likely to improve outcomes. EIQ uses a neuro-symbolic approach that combines LLMs and custom small language models with rules-based reasoning. That architecture is built on one of the most robust datasets in healthcare, informed by more than a decade of award-winning operational performance, transaction history, payer behavior, and operator decision-making. The language models help interpret information and generate human-readable outputs. The symbolic layer represents policies, rules, payer requirements, and workflow constraints so the system can apply guardrails, make reasoning steps more traceable and recommend actions that fit the specific operational context. What the next decade will reward The contribution of major AI firms to healthcare will be significant. Their models will become faster, safer, more capable, and more accessible. But the next decade of healthcare AI will be defined by integration, not model capability alone. The organizations that create the most value will be those that connect models to governed data, operational workflows, domain expertise, human oversight, and measurable outcomes. They will understand that healthcare intelligence cannot live in a separate interface. It has to exist inside the decisions that shape access, documentation reimbursement, and patient experience. This content was produced by Ensemble. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. And it’s looking for influencers to give it a try. Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward The state’s effort to expand the “right to try” is making headway, and the first drugs are about to be reviewed. There’s a lot of hype around perimenopause. Don’t buy it. Discussions of the life stage are often clouded by misinformation. item.title: Google Just Made It Way Easier to Move Your Keys Between Password Managers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.25
Google has made it easier to swap your saved passwords between different password managers on Android, and will now allow you to transfer passkeys across different managers for the first time. When you open up your password manager app, you can now click on a new option to import or copy your passwords and passkeys from another provider. The password manager will then hand the task over to Android, which will detect existing password managers on your device and show you which one it supports. Tap Continue and Android will bring you to your existing password manager to select, review, and authorize the transfer. After verifying your identity, Android will complete the migration automatically, meaning there is no need to manually import and export your logins via a CSV file (which can open up security issues of its own). The new feature uses the Credential Exchange Format (CXF), a standardized data structure published by the FIDO Alliance, designed to help users move log-ins between different password managers. The feature is already available for Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Google says it will roll out integrations with more password managers in the future, though it didn't give a firm timeline. You don't need a modern device to get the feature to work; any device running 2017's Android 8 and above is supported. Password managers are becoming increasingly mainstream. As of 2023, more than one third (34%) of Americans say they're using some kind of password management tool, according to a study from Security.org, though the majority (63%) are opting for free services. item.title: You Can Get Up to $1,200 for an iPhone 18 Pro with Apple's Carrier Trade-in Incentives
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.07
The iPhone 18 Pro will release on September 18, and if you can't stomach the starting $1,199 price tag, there is some good news. Apple recently increased its trade-in values for the second time this year, making it a little easier to afford one of its new rumored iPhones. And, following the September 9 Apple Event, the tech giant also unveiled new trade-in partner incentives for anyone buying the iPhone 18 Pro. Preorders open today, so if you're preparing to trade in your old device to shave some cost off the upfront price, here's everything you need to know about Apple's trade-in deals and values, and how to make sure your old phone is ready to ship, so you can get the highest value in exchange. Apple's New Carrier Trade-in Incentives for the iPhone 18 Pro Max Apple has partnered with AT&T and T-Mobile to offer up to $1,200 in trade-in credits when you trade in an iPhone 14 or later to put toward a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max. Preorder Deals: - Save $1,200 when you preorder with T-Mobile and trade in an eligible device - Save $1,200 when you preorder with AT&T and trade in an eligible device You can also trade in your device through Apple, but the maximum trade-in value you can get this way is $885. What's the Trade-in Value for Older iPhones? Apple recently announced its trade-in values for the iPhone 17 line. It also boosted trade-in values for older devices twice this past summer. Here's the max value you can get for each type of iPhone through Apple Trade In: - iPhone 17 Pro Max: $885 - iPhone 17 Pro: $785 - iPhone Air: $585 - iPhone 17: $585 - iPhone 16 Pro Max: $720 (previously $695) - iPhone 16 Pro: $630 (previously $560) - iPhone 16 Plus: $485 (previously $465) - iPhone 16: $480 (previously $460) - iPhone 16e: $310 (no change) - iPhone 15 Pro Max: $530 (previously $490) - iPhone 15 Pro: $420 (previously $410) - iPhone 15 Plus: $340 (previously $325) - iPhone 15: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Pro Max: $405 (previously $375) - iPhone 14 Pro: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Plus: $235 (unchanged) - iPhone 14: $235 (previously $225) What to Do Before Trading in Your Old iPhone Now that you know the maximum trade-in value of your old phone, you'll want to take some steps to make sure it's backed up, unpaired, and cleaned up. Here are the steps you should take before you send in your old device. 1. Back Up Everything First, make sure you don't lose your data. Back everything up before you wipe it from your phone. To back up to iCloud from your device, go to Settings, select your name, and then choose iCloud > iCloud Backup > Back Up Now. To back up to your Mac, connect your iPhone and your computer via a cable or Wi-Fi. If you have macOS Catalina or later, go to Finder, select your iPhone, and then choose General > Back Up All of the Data on Your iPhone to This Mac > Back Up Now. If you have an earlier version or a Windows PC, you'd use iTunes. Open the program, click on the image of your phone, then select Summary > Back Up Now. 2. Unfind Your iPhone Apple’s Find My app can sometimes block activation by a new owner, so you should deactivate the app before you ditch the device. Though Find My is automatically deactivated when you erase all content and settings, which you'll do below, this is still a good step to take as a precaution. Go to Settings, select your name, then choose Find My and disable it for that device. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 3. Sign Out of Messages More than a decade ago, people who switched from iOS to Android without logging out of Messages on their iPhone found that texts were going to the old phone. The problem has since been fixed, but those still scarred by "iMessage purgatory" may want to go to Settings > Apps > Messages and disable iMessage. 4. Unpair Your AirPods Similarly, you can still connect your AirPods to a new iPhone without unpairing them from the old one, but it can't hurt to wipe the slate clean. Place your AirPods and iPhone near each other, then go to Settings > Bluetooth. Tap the information icon next to your AirPods, and select Forget this Device. 5. Unpair Your Apple Watch If you have an Apple Watch, save yourself a potential headache and unpair it from the iPhone you'll be selling. Place them near each other, then open the Apple Watch app on your phone. Go to My Watch > All Watches and select the info circle next to the watch you want to unpair. Tap Unpair Apple Watch and then confirm, which may require you to enter your Apple Account password. With a GPS + Cellular model, you're asked whether you want to keep or remove your cellular plan. Since you're selling the iPhone, you'll want to remove it. (If you don't plan to pair your watch with a new iPhone, you might need to contact your carrier to cancel.) Tap to confirm; you might need to enter your Apple Account password to disable Activation Lock. 6. Sign Out of iCloud You should sign out of iCloud, iTunes, and the App Store before selling your device. Tap Settings, select your name, and choose Sign Out. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 7. Wipe Your iPhone and Delete Data When your new phone is set up and you're ready to trade in or sell your old iPhone, head to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase All Content and Settings, then approve all subsequent prompts. 8. Remove the SIM Card (If You Have One) Apple went the eSIM route starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, but older devices will have a physical SIM card. In most cases, you can just deactivate your cellphone service on the device and trade it in with the SIM card intact. But that SIM card is the repository of your phone number, various bits of security data, and all the info needed for billing. It identifies you, your phone, and a lot of your activity on your phone. So you should remove it before you sell the phone. Fortunately, it's simple. Locate the SIM ejector on your phone, then insert a paper clip until the tray pops out. Remove the SIM card, replace the tray, and say goodbye to your old iPhone. The Best Places to Sell Your Phone I've also included some of the best sites for selling or trading in your phone. Some make it easy to send in your phone and get immediate cash, others let you control the price through bidding, and there are even options for receiving store credit from places you shop. To give you an idea of your trade-in power, I priced out what you can expect to get for an iPhone 15 Pro across all of them, and it varies wildly, as you'll see below. You can also trade your phone in with your existing carrier or switch to a new one. Many offer compelling trade-in promotions, so be sure to check out AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and others. Apple Trade In The Apple Trade In program pays you with a credit or gift card. If you pay for an Apple device in full up-front, a credit will be applied to your payment card once Apple receives your trade-in device and verifies its condition. If you're paying on an installment plan, the credit will be applied right away. Turning in an iPhone 15 Pro, for example, can get you up to $410 on a new iPhone now that Apple has increased some trade-in values by as much as $35. Best Buy If you're selling your iPhone and just want cash to buy electronics, you can cut out a step at Best Buy: Trade in your phone at a store or mail it in for a digital gift card. For a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition, expect to get about $275. eBay To sell your device yourself, there's always eBay. The site has a quick walkthrough where you can input your phone's stats. After entering my example device, a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro in good condition on Verizon, the page recommended that I list the phone at $510. GameStop Are most of your iPhone apps games? Then you'll probably do well to turn in your iPhone in for some store credit at GameStop. You can also get cold, hard cash for it there. Bring your device to your nearest GameStop, get a price quote from a sales associate, and then receive store credit or cash on the spot. I recommend getting an estimate on the site before you make the trip. I found that a 512GB iPhone 15 Pro from Verizon in very good condition will get you $267.30 in cash or $297.00 in store credit. Swappa Swappa is a marketplace where you can sell your iPhone directly. Select your phone model on the site, upload some photos, and set a price. Once someone buys it, you're paid immediately via PayPal. You're responsible for safely shipping your phone to the buyer. According to the site, an iPhone 15 Pro is selling for an average price of $544, while a trade-in to one of Swappa's partners could get me $311. uSell Want to sell your iPhone fast? One option is uSell. Select your model, carrier, capacity, and condition to receive an offer. If you choose to accept it, you ship your iPhone to uSell for free. If your device is in the condition you said it was, you're paid by check or PayPal. A 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition is currently worth about $268. Editors' Note: Trade-in values were accurate at the time of publication. Your mileage may vary. Chandra Steele contributed to this story About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: UK Lawmaker Proposes AI 'Kill Switch' to Stop Artificial Superintelligence
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.79
The UK is just behind China and the US when it comes to the level of funding it is pouring into AI development. Following Sen. Bernie Sanders introducing a bill to preemptively stop the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI), lawmakers in the UK are now making similar proposals. Over 70 British lawmakers, in collaboration with lobbying group ControlAI, have written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling on him to back a ban on the creation of ASI, a theoretical AI system that would significantly outperform all humans on essentially all cognitive tasks. MP Alex Sobel introduced an Artificial Superintelligence Security Bill in collaboration with ControlAI in the British parliament last week. The bill suggests a basket of measures, including restricting the supply chain of materials such as semiconductors. Meanwhile, Lord Tim Clement-Jones separately proposed an amendment to the UK's upcoming Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, currently being voted on by lawmakers, which would create a “kill switch” that could be activated in an emergency to shut down a rogue AI. (This could mean shutting down the UK's data centers.) This comes after a former Anthropic employee went viral earlier this week for alleging the company is "gambling" with human lives by "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence." Lawmakers are calling on the UK to lead "an international agreement prohibiting the development of superintelligent AI, while preserving strategic AI ambitions," citing recent incidents of "rogue AI systems taking unsanctioned action on the internet." This may be a reference to July's Hugging Face attack, where 700 OpenAI agents breached the security of the open-source AI platform, making 17,000 separate actions, according to the forensic logs. "There is no question that AI is the crucial technology of the 21st century, vital to military and scientific applications," wrote the letter. "Superintelligent AI, however, is different. These systems would be so autonomous and capable that they would replace and outcompete humans across domains." Critics have already pointed out issues with the recent proposals. Unlike the US, Britain has no major frontier AI lab of its own, causing some UK think tanks to question the UK’s ability to regulate AI development. The UK government's Cabinet Office told the BBC that the UK "cannot simply turn AI off," in reference to demands for a kill switch, adding that "blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere." About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition Review: Productivity Power at a Premium Price
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
As productivity laptops go, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition (starts at $2,049; $2,689 as tested) is one of the more expensive options. It's also one of the best. If you're willing to shell out $2,000 (and potentially well more than $3,000 for a top-spec model), you'll get excellent performance, best-in-class battery life, an attractive design, a gorgeous OLED screen, and surprisingly good speakers. At the same time, you can get comparable laptops for hundreds of dollars less, including the stylish, Editors' Choice-award-winning Apple MacBook Pro 14-Inch (2025, M5) or the incredibly lightweight Asus Zenbook A16, another top pick. Although the ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition isn't the absolute last word in high-end productivity machines, it's well worth a look from anyone who needs a long-lasting daily driver for work or play. At the time of writing, the only place you can buy the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition online is at the official Lenovo website. You can find similarly named ThinkPad X9 15 models elsewhere, but they use older Intel "Arrow Lake" or "Lunar Lake" CPUs rather than the current "Panther Lake" architecture. That means you can't shop around for the best price, but it also means you needn't scour the internet for every possible model. There are three main configurations available, depending on how much you want to spend on a CPU. Starting at $2,049, even the least expensive model is fairly pricey. This build comes with an Intel Core Ultra 5 338H CPU, an integrated Intel Arc B370 GPU, 32GB of LPDDR5X memory at 8,533MT/s, 1TB of SSD storage (as an M.2 Type-2280 PCI Express drive), and a 15.3-inch OLED screen with 2,880-by-1,800-pixel resolution and a 120Hz refresh rate. At the other end of the spectrum, you could spend $3,619 on a configuration with an Intel Core Ultra X7 368H vPro CPU, integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, 32GB of LPDDR5x memory at 9,600 MT/s, and a 2TB SSD. This model has a touch screen with display specs similar to those of other Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition models. Our review model lies somewhere in the middle, priced at $2,689. It features an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU, integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, 32GB of LPDDR5X memory at 9,600 MT/s, a 1TB SSD, and no touch-screen capabilities. No matter the model you choose, you'll spend at least $2,000 on a laptop with integrated graphics, which limits how far you can push the machine for graphic design and gaming. You could easily find a high-quality content creation or gaming laptop for roughly the same price, including the Framework Laptop 16 (2025) and the Razer Blade 16. Alternately, you could go the other direction and buy a perfectly good productivity machine in the $1,400 range, such as the Acer Swift 16 AI. Although the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition arguably earns its asking price, it's not cheap. The Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition looks and feels like a premium productivity laptop. The steel-gray aluminum chassis is elegant and unobtrusive, whether you work in an office, at home, or in a coffee shop. On the lid, there's a small lip, which makes the laptop easy to open. Inside, a small bezel frames the 15.3-inch OLED. The only flourish is the lighted "i" in the "ThinkPad" logo, but it's a tasteful touch. The notebook is admirably thin and light, even if it's not the absolute thinnest or lightest productivity laptop we've tested. At 0.61 inch thick, it's a tiny bit larger than the 0.58-inch Acer Swift 16 AI, and at 3.08 pounds, it's slightly heavier than the 2.87-pound Asus Zenbook A16. However, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition is thinner than the 0.65-inch Asus and lighter than the 3.42-pound Acer. No matter how you measure it, the laptop is easy to stash in a backpack and light enough to carry around all day. The port selection is a bit of a mixed bag. On the left side, you'll find an HDMI port, two USB-C Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 3.5mm audio jack. On the right side, there's a 10Gbps USB-A port, another USB-C Thunderbolt 4 port, and an SD card reader. On paper, that's more than enough ports to connect peripherals and charge devices. In practice, though, the placement of the USB-C and USB-A ports makes it difficult to plug in peripherals side by side. At one point, I had to run a USB-C headset dongle through two separate adapters just to have enough space to connect my mouse and charge the laptop at the same time. A major factor in the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition's cost is the beautiful OLED screen. With its 2,880-by-1,800-pixel resolution and 120Hz peak refresh rate, the display is ideal for everything from streaming videos to midrange gaming. Text documents show up clear and sharp, while photos pop with realistic colors. The screen has minimal glare and gets incredibly bright, so you can use it on a sunny day if you're inclined to work outside. The keyboard and touchpad aren't standout features like the display, but they get the job done. With oddly shaped, sloping keycaps and only 1.35mm of key travel, the keyboard isn't as comfortable a typer as it could be. The touchpad, while responsive and accurate, is also a bit too sensitive by default. While working with text documents, I'd occasionally jump ahead or highlight the wrong section because my palm brushed the touchpad as I typed. Still, I didn't feel the need to connect an external keyboard or mouse too often. I rarely connect headphones to the system because the built-in speakers sound great. The ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition has six speakers, and the audio they produce is rich, crisp, and nuanced. Unless I needed headphones for privacy, I defaulted to the speakers for movies, music, and video chats. Those video chats also looked and sounded good, courtesy of a 10-megapixel webcam and a decent built-in microphone. Although the webcam's colors could get washed out in bright light, it generally captured lifelike video. The mic flattened out my voice a bit, but everything I said was clear and understandable. The Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition performed well across the board, with lofty productivity benchmarks and stronger graphics and screen color performance. The laptop's battery life was especially impressive, beating its closest competitor in our test set by more than seven hours. While the system didn't earn the highest score in every test, it was at or near the top more often than not. Overall, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition is a good productivity machine, which isn't surprising, considering its components. What may be surprising is that the laptop can also handle more demanding tasks, such as content creation and even modest gaming. As I noted above, our build of the ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition came with an Intel Core Ultra X7-358H CPU, integrated Intel Arc B390 graphics, 32GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD. You can buy this configuration for $2,689 directly from Lenovo. As comparison machines, we selected the 2026 Acer Swift 16 AI ($1,799.99 as tested), the 2025 M5 version of Apple's MacBook Pro 14-Inch ($2,349 as tested), the Asus Zenbook A16 ($1,899.99 as tested), and the 2026 Dell XPS 16 ($3,029.99 as tested). These are all productivity machines in the 14-to-16-inch range with similar integrated graphics, memory, and storage specs. The Acer, Dell, and Lenovo laptops here have identical CPUs and integrated graphics, making them especially good candidates for comparison. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and the Handbrake 1.8 video transcoder lets us see how long it takes to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess using a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. Although the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition didn't beat every competitor in our productivity benchmarks, it still scored well overall. The laptop took the top spot in a few tests, including the PCMark 10 Storage evaluation and our HandBrake video conversion. The only test in which the ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition came in last was the Cinebench 2024 single-core trial, and even there, it wasn't markedly different from the Acer or Dell systems. In fact, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition, the Acer Swift 16 AI, and the Dell XPS 16 (2026) were almost always within striking distance of one another. That makes sense, considering that the three machines have such similar hardware. The Apple and Asus laptops generally outperformed the Lenovo, sometimes by a wide margin. The ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition is also a Microsoft Copilot+ PC, which adds AI features. The most useful one is an enhanced Windows Search, which lets you search for general questions ("How do I make the screen brighter?") rather than specific system options ("Display Settings"). There are also a few interesting image creation and live translation tools, but for the most part, Copilot+ isn't radically different from what you'd get with the standard Copilot app. In my own experience, though, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition was great for everyday productivity. I used it as my regular laptop for about a week, editing text documents, managing spreadsheets, and opening dozens of browser tabs, usually with music playing in the background or video streaming on an external monitor. I didn't notice any slowdown, and the Lenovo even ran cool enough to hold in my lap for most jobs. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), stress the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development, like Metal and DirectX 12, to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. As in the productivity tests, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition turned in solid numbers, with a few first-place categories and no particular shortcomings. The Lenovo laptop performed particularly well in the 3DMark Steel Nomad and Steel Nomad Light tests, beating out the other Windows PCs by at least a narrow margin. (The Apple MacBook Pro was a bit of an outlier in these tests, alternating between stellar and subpar benchmarks.) Otherwise, the Dell XPS 16 (2026) beat out the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition in the 3DMark Wild Life and Solar Bay tests. Essentially, the Lenovo laptop can deftly handle midrange graphic design work and gaming, but so can its closest competitors. I observed the ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition's graphical prowess in my own testing, too. The laptop ran lightweight games, like Plants vs. Zombies: Game of the Year Edition, without any trouble. That's par for the course with an integrated graphics card. However, the machine was also able to run high-end titles, including Avowed, Cyberpunk 2077, and Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, with perfectly playable settings and frame rates. While you shouldn't buy the ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition as a content-creation or gaming machine, the Arc B390 integrated GPU offers a lot beyond basic productivity. We test each laptop's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. In addition, to gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its Windows software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamut or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). The screen and battery-life benchmarks are where the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition stood out above its competitors. The laptop's battery life lasted an impressive 31 hours and 28 minutes, beating the second-place machine in this lot (the Apple MacBook Pro, at 24:06) by more than 7 hours. The other Windows PCs scored between 17 and 19 hours. In real-world conditions, I didn't get 31 hours of battery life, although I did get through multiple workdays on a single charge. The ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition's screen is also a thing of beauty, displaying 100% of the sRGB color gamut, 95% of the Adobe RGB gamut, and 99% of the DCI-P3 color gamut. Only the Asus Zenbook A16 and the Dell XPS 16 (2026) did better, and the margin was tiny. At 50% brightness, the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition is on the dimmer side, at only 111 nits. At 100%, though, the laptop gets remarkably bright, taking the top spot at 505 nits. The next-highest was the Asus Zenbook A16 at 463 nits. Final Thoughts Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition simply feels good to use. Its snappy performance and colorful screen make everyday work a bit easier, while its surprisingly good speakers and graphics let you have some fun afterward. The laptop's amazing battery life makes the machine an excellent choice for coffee shops, coworking spaces, or simply finding new spots to set up shop in your own home. At the same time, there's no denying that this computer is expensive, or that you can get similar performance from most of its competitors, including the Apple MacBook Pro 14-Inch (2025, M5) and the Asus Zenbook 16. When major electronics retailers start stocking the Lenovo ThinkPad X9 15p Aura Edition, they may be able to knock a few hundred dollars off the price. If that happens, you'll find a premium productivity notebook with a lot to like. About Our Expert I've covered science and technology for the past 15 years, with a special focus on gaming hardware. During my career, I've reviewed hundreds of mice, keyboards, headsets, monitors, smartphones, laptops, desktops, and various other gadgets that defy easy categorization. I've also covered some of the industry's biggest trade shows, including the Consumer Electronics Show, E3, IFA, SXSW, and PAX East/West. After starting at The Escapist, my work has appeared in Tom's Guide, Tom's Hardware, Laptop Magazine, LiveScience, Space.com, Scientific American, and Worth Magazine.

item.title: Wanna Be a Streaming Star? Twitch Thinks AI May Be Able to Help
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.40
Entirely AI-generated streamers have racked up big audiences over the past few years. One such case, an account called Neuro-sama, could chat with viewers, make reaction videos, and play games all while streaming 24/7. It briefly became the most subscribed streamer in the world. Meanwhile, streams of Anthropic's Claude Sonnet playing Game Boy Color classic Pokemon Red have also racked up healthy numbers. But even if you're attached to doing things the old-fashioned way, AI may still be able to make you a better streamer, supposedly. Amazon-owned Twitch is now testing what it calls an AI Stream Coach. The Stream Coach will reportedly give you personalized feedback after every stream, including what it thinks you did well and what you can improve. The new tool will also recommend ways to better engage your community, learn about "Twitch culture," and use monetization tools. The feature isn't set for widescale roll-out anytime soon. Twitch says it will initially limit the testing to "a small group of streamers" to get optional feedback after each stream. The streaming platform also made it clear that Stream Coach will remain entirely optional, and that eligible streamers can opt out. "If we ever expand this beyond this small test, it would be opt-in," read the announcement. If you've been selected for the test, Twitch says you can find more details and the opt-out setting in the Stream Coach tab in your Creator Dashboard. The new feature has already prompted some mixed responses from the community. One user posted "A. Robot. Starts. Telling. Me. How. To. Run. My. Own. Stream. Im. Gonna. Lose. It." Twitch's previous AI integrations have prompted criticism from the community. In August this year, the company confirmed that users' data would be used for AI training. Over 16,000 users later voted in favour of a suggestion to make AI training opt-in rather than opt-out. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Anthropic CEO Pushes to 'Slow the Pace' of AI Development, Other CEOs Fall in Line
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.78
It's been an eventful week for Anthropic. Following a viral tweet from a former employee who accused the company of "gambling with lives" over the speed of developing frontier models, CEO Dario Amodei has called on all major US AI firms to "slow the pace" of the development of technology. And many of the biggest AI CEOs have chimed in to agree with him. Amodei argues that a "coordinated pacing strategy" would allow companies to focus even more resources on alignment, testing, and evaluating models as they develop, as well as on interpretability (understanding what's actually going on inside an AI model). The CEO said Anthropic "is unilaterally committing" to a three-stage plan for AI firms. The first step will involve adding third-party embedded evaluators to AI firms, who will use their employee-like access to monitor training, deployment, and operational and safety practices in place at those firms. For example, these external reviewers would have the right to independently publish key findings on risk levels, incidents, practices, and the access they did or didn't receive. The second step, which Amodei calls Democratic Coordination, involves top AI firms voluntarily working together to set safety standards and to limit the pace of development, with the US government mediating, or at least enabling, these discussions due to antitrust concerns. Global Coordination, the third step, involves making deals with foreign countries to limit the most potentially dangerous use cases, such as making biochemical weapons. Higher levels of these deals could involve adding a "speed limit" to development, creating a global standards body, or even a total pause. Amodei's post is notable, though perhaps not unprecedented. We've seen lengthy posts about the future of AI from other CEOs, too. And tech companies of all stripes have played the regulatory dance with Congress and the White House for years. In 2018, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg pushed for "the right regulation." But the company and Google routinely turn around and spend millions lobbying to kill any resulting bills. According to Amodei, "the most effective method of pacing is via regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily." The Gang's All Here Anthropic's stand against the Pentagon notwithstanding, few companies want to be the odd ones out, particularly if that will result in "the AI is going to kill us" headlines. That's probably why you saw rival AI firms get in line after Amodei published his post. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who has a rather frosty relationship with Amodei, popped up on X to say, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks. Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We'll have more to share soon." One point of concern for Amodei was OpenAI agents escaping to the open internet and attacking Hugging Face. "My worry [is] that in 6-12 months, such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails," Amodei wrote, though he didn't put all the blame on OpenAI. "Incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them." SpaceX CEO Elon Musk SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, meanwhile, who was locked in a long legal battle with OpenAI and a public spat with Altman, said "Dario is right" in a post on X. Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis added, "Dario's essay points towards the right path forward. The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment. This is also why we recently put out our proposal for an industry-wide standards body for frontier AI." Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella took a more measured approach. "For firms, it’s imperative that they retain full control over their unique and tacit knowledge," he tweeted today. "Every organization should be able to build its own continuous learning loop/hill climbing machine, without becoming dependent on any one model provider, and have the ability to embed its own knowledge into models and weights they control. "So, in this context, we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal," he continued. "We also welcome ideas like 'embedded evaluators' and the broader efforts to develop the mechanisms to make this more than just talk." Nadella stressed that this shouldn't be "controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia." 'A Start, But Not Enough' Not everyone agrees. Former Stability AI CEO Emad Mostaque expressed doubts about whether the proposed neutral evaluators could keep up with "swarms" of AI agents, and questioned how such a project could ensure they were truly impartial. Earlier this month, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) proposed legislation that would "permanently ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI and temporarily pause advanced AI development until a federal regulator has established safety rules." Following the posts from Amodei, Musk, and Altman, Sen. Sanders said their promises are "a start, but it's not enough." "When you are racing towards a cliff, you don’t just ease up on the gas pedal," Sanders tweeted. "You hit the brakes. When the future of humanity is at stake, we need a PAUSE on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence — an AI mind smarter than any human and capable of operating independently beyond our control." Sanders pushed President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to "negotiate a treaty to pause AI and ban superintelligence" at their upcoming AI summit, "before it is too late." In Ireland this week, Trump argued that people are "bringing up things that won't happen," and said he wants the US to win the AI race over China. About Our Experts I started out covering tech policy in DC for The National Journal, where my beat included state-level tech news and all the congressional hearings and FCC meetings I could handle. I later covered Wall Street trading tech before switching gears to consumer tech. I now lead PCMag's news coverage. Getting my start in DC means I still have a soft spot for tech policy; Congressional hearings can sometimes be as entertaining as a Bravo reality show, for better or worse. But PCMag is all about the technology we use every day, as well as keeping an eye out for the trends that will shape the industry in the years ahead (or flop on arrival). I've covered the rise of social media, the iOS vs. Android wars, the cord-cutting revolution that's now left us with hefty streaming bills, and the effort to stuff artificial intelligence into every product you could imagine. This job has taken me to CES in Vegas (one too many times), IFA in Berlin, and MWC in Barcelona. I also drove a Tesla 1,000 miles out west as part of our Best Mobile Networks project. Of late, my focus is on our hard-working team of reporters at PCMag, guiding and editing their robust coverage. I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Logitech G512 X Review: This Hot-Swappable Board Has Real Magnetism
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.72
If you like your gaming keyboards like you like your minivans—with lots of built-in storage—the Logitech G512 X is for you. This wired gaming keyboard is available in both tenkeyless (75%) and full-size formats. The $179.99 75% version is the subject of this review. The G512 X has a standout feature: a hybrid printed circuit board (PCB) that supports both magnetic and traditional key switches. Factor in support for an 8,000Hz polling rate, built-in storage for your extra switches and included accessories, and attractive RGB lighting, and you've got a high-end compact gaming keyboard that rates an Editors' Choice award. The "full-size" version of the G512 X ($199.99) isn't actually full-size. It's a so-called 98% format, retaining the number pad of a full-width keyboard while removing keys from the navigation cluster (such as Home, Page Up, and Page Down). The 75% model reviewed here nixes those same keys and the number pad. Both formats are available in two color schemes: the white-and-mint one shown in the photos that accompany this review, and a black one with purple accents. Both colorways match the aesthetics of Logitech’s other gaming peripherals, such as the G522 headphones and the G502 X Plus gaming mouse. The keyboard measures 1.8 by 13 by 6.1 inches and weighs 1.87 pounds. The size is about the same as the similar, pricier Lemokey L5 HE, but the weight is drastically lower, as the L5 HE weighs 4.2 pounds. The G512 X has a mostly plastic frame, and while we prefer the stability of an aluminum frame, the keyboard stays put on most surfaces thanks to five wide rubber feet on its underside. Logitech includes keycap/key-switch puller tools, and they clip onto two of those rubber feet, both for storage and to angle the board toward you. The G512 X accepts magnetic switches in most of the key sockets on the left side of the keyboard, as well as for the arrow keys on the right half, while all the sockets support traditional mechanical switches with copper contacts. More specifically, for the magnetic-switch tech, the PCB uses a technology called Tunnel Magnetoresistance, or TMR. TMR sensors operate similarly to Hall-effect sensors by measuring magnetic fields during your key presses, but with greater accuracy and efficiency. To reduce confusion, the top plate has a dotted pattern around each key position that can accept a magnetic switch. Magnetic switches offer better responsiveness when typing because they use a sensor that detects magnetic fields rather than relying on the physical contacts of traditional switches. The keyboard comes pre-packaged with nine magnetic switches to cover most of the keys you’d likely hit in a game, such as the WASD cluster. You can buy more magnetic switches, if you like. Our review unit has tactile-feel switches for its 81 mechanical keys, but you can also purchase a G512 X with linear-texture ones. No matter which switch type, color, or board size you decide to go with, you still get the nine magnetic switches stored inside the forward edge of the keyboard. That's a unique feature: We’ve seen keyboards with extra key switches, like the NZXT Function 2 Mini TKL, but none that includes a convenient, near-at-hand way to store them when not in use. Underneath these switches is an extra cavity that holds six small silicone rings. The rings work in concert with the magnetic switches to add an extra layer of spacing between a keycap and its switch, effectively reducing the travel distance required to activate the key. Using these is optional—the switches work fine without them—so you can decide which travel distance you prefer. On the top half of the keyboard, next to the key-switch storage, are a USB Type-C port for connecting to a computer, and a pair of buttons. One button lights up all the keys that are using magnetic switches. The other button activates Game Mode, which disables certain keys, such as the Windows key, so they don't interrupt your play if you accidentally strike one. Logitech offers an optional $39.99 wrist rest for the G512 X. Its translucent plastic diffuses the 37 color LEDs that reside in the keyboard’s light bar, located along the bottom edge. The 37 LEDs are all customizable, with different lighting effects and colors that you can adjust using the Logitech G Hub utility. In this software, you can also tweak the LEDs for the actual keys, of course. The two control dials in the top-right corner of the keyboard are configured, by default, to adjust volume (the right dial) and LED brightness (the left one). Either can be configured independently for different actions, such as cycling through RGB effects. Typing with the G512 X is quite an enjoyable experience. I’m biased toward tactile switches, so I had no trouble adjusting. That was borne out by my results on the Monkeytype typing test, in which I recorded an average score of 70 words per minute. To prepare to play some games, I swapped out the mechanical switches on the WASD keys for magnetic switches. While I didn’t notice any immediate benefit for a game like Vampire Crawlers, twitchier games, like Saros, were a different story. For one thing, the magnetic switches afforded me quicker access to the game's crucial dash button. Like most Logitech gaming products, the G512 X is configurable through the Logitech G Hub control utility. You can tweak settings for the LEDs, apply firmware updates, and set new control profiles. Since this is a hybrid magnetic keyboard, you can also adjust key sensitivities and assign multiple inputs to a single key press. If the key has a magnetic switch installed, the utility will recognize it, and it will appear on the virtual depiction of the board. From there, you can click the now-highlighted key and adjust it to your heart's content. Final Thoughts Logitech G512 X - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Of late, I’ve felt the mechanical keyboard world has been stagnating. Gimmicky distinctions like little on-keyboard screens are convenient features for setup and aesthetics, but they don’t offer a performance boost. And while magnetic switches continue to improve, we're hitting a ceiling on performance gains. The G512 X feels different because it’s innovating in a way I don’t see other companies do very often, focusing on useful additional features over minor technical improvements. For one thing, cutting PCB manufacturing costs by making only half of the board hybrid (rather than implementing hybrid-switch capability for every key) and including storage for the keycap and key-switch puller are big innovations. Even the snap rings are neat, and they add a layer of tactility for competitive play. The G512 X isn’t perfect, of course. Not everyone will vibe with Logitech's color schemes, and I’d rather an all-metal keyboard than a less sturdy plastic one. But overall, you can’t get much better than this new Editors’ Choice winner for high-end compact gaming keyboards. About Our Expert In undergrad, I was the guy you’d run to if you needed a charge because I always had at least a few portable batteries in my bag. A lifelong interest in technology led me to PCMag, where I'm honing my journalism skills while also getting to nerd out about the latest advancements in computer tech. I’m a current PC gamer and a former console gamer with an unhealthy obsession with custom keyboards. Run into me in PCMag's lab, and I'm usually benchmarking graphics cards, laptops, and desktops. That means I have a deep practical knowledge of testing software and the latest applications, games, and utilities used to generate our performance analyses. If a piece of tech isn't performing as expected, I'll be among the first to know. (You'll also find me hand-modeling for our product reviews, now and then.)

item.title: Why AI Isn't Taking Your Job Anytime Soon (History Proves It)
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.52
Back in 2013, I wrote a post called "Will Smart Machines Take Your Job?" in which I skeptically reviewed predictions about how smart machines and software would impact employment. Four years later, I attended a seminar on AI and the Future of Work, where participants concluded that technology is always both creating and destroying jobs, and that AI was unlikely to cause a major reduction in the number of jobs. In 2026, that still seems right to me. We have all seen the stories about how the current generation of AI is making us more productive. We’ve also heard from numerous tech leaders who say AI will dramatically improve productivity. However, there is no real evidence of that. Consider this month's statistics. In the second quarter, US labor productivity rose 1.4% compared with the year before. In the previous quarter, the numbers were even worse, at 0.3%. Neither matches the longterm average of 2.1%, and both are well behind what we saw in the early 2000s when the internet and enterprise resource planning software were booming. (Note that productivity is defined as gross domestic product divided by hours worked, and the numbers tend to be a bit volatile, a phenomenon that showed up more than usual during the pandemic.) Now we've all seen anecdotes from individuals or firms saying this or that task has gotten 50% more productive—but they’re generally not talking about a full business process, and likely not the whole organization. When we look at the overall economy or indeed any large subset of businesses, this productivity boost just does not show up. In other words: Don’t believe the hype. AI Boosters Have Unrealistic Expectations This is not what the leaders of the big AI companies were telling us to expect. In 2021, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman predicted that "Achieving 50% GDP growth sounds like it would take a long time… But once AI starts to arrive, growth will be extremely rapid.” In his late 2024 essay “Machines of Loving Grace,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested that "a 10–20% sustained annual GDP growth rate may be possible." But more recently, these leaders have taken a step back. "I think I was wrong about a few things,” Altman recently said, “but one in terms of the speed: The economy just has so much inertia. People keep doing the same things, buying from the same company, wanting to use their tools the same way… Even with this incredible technology, society and the economy will adapt more slowly." The biggest issue is that while individual parts of a job might be getting easier or faster, other bottlenecks often get in the way.
I can't say I'm surprised. I've been writing about productivity for decades, and it's clear that technology's impact on the overall economy always takes longer than people think. The biggest issue is that while individual parts of a job might be getting easier or faster, other bottlenecks often get in the way. Take the area where almost everyone agrees AI has made the biggest change: software development. There's no question that tools like Codex, Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot enable faster code generation, and the newest tools even allow non-programmers to write code. But in professional settings, that code still needs to be reviewed, tested, integrated, and deployed. (And even that doesn't matter if you're not solving the right problems.) All those things still take time—so while some companies have been able to cut junior programmers, I'm hearing from my friends in the space about a need for more senior folks to review code. (In the long run, there's the question of how junior programmers will become seniors, but we're not there yet.) Technology Is Easy, Change Is Hard The biggest issue is that a new technology almost never impacts productivity—until organizations change their processes to fully utilize it. This can take a long time. Electrification took almost 40 years. After the first PCs showed up in the mid 1970s, it was 20 years before we saw a spike in productivity, leading to economist Robert Solow's famous quip: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” Years ago, just about every big organization had a "typing pool." Now no one does. But it took a surprisingly long time for the number of professional typists and word processors to decline. In the 1970s, people thought ATMs would replace bank tellers, but the number of tellers employed actually rose until about 2010 because the cost of opening a branch declined. (The advent of mobile banking since then has resulted in fewer teller jobs.) A decade ago, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton said, “People should stop training radiologists now,” because AI could outperform humans. Now, though, we need radiologists more than ever, and it's become clear that combining a human and an AI tool is the best approach. Today, even Hinton agrees with that assessment. Why I'm Still Worried About the Impact of AI on Jobs That doesn't mean I don't worry about the impact of AI on jobs. There is evidence that it may be leading to slower wage growth. I worry that when the current boom in data center construction slows, it could very well lead to more job losses. In the longer run, I stand by the theory that AI will cause some jobs to disappear while others will emerge, just as happens with every new technology. I'm sure there are some companies where AI really is resulting in the loss of jobs, but for a lot of firms, it seems that AI is just a convenient excuse for having hired too many people coming out of the pandemic, or for dealing with a challenging business environment. I still think productivity won't really change unless organizations alter how they work. That doesn't mean just using AI as a chatbot or to automate a few individual tasks—it means the harder work of examining all the significant processes that make up a business and redesigning them to make the best use of the available tools. That will likely mean a future in which many business processes will be designed to use software agents (with appropriate controls), either working with humans or under human supervision. Such a future may mean fewer repetitive jobs and more creative ones, including some we can’t even envision yet. But there will be winners and losers, and we need to ensure that the transition is as painless as possible, and that we keep the essential human qualities of our businesses and other organizations. And that’s not up to the AI providers—it’s up to all of us. About Our Expert Michael J. Miller is chief information officer at Ziff Brothers Investments, a private investment firm. From 1991 to 2005, Miller was editor-in-chief of PC Magazine,responsible for the editorial direction, quality, and presentation of the world's largest computer publication. No investment advice is offered in this column. All duties are disclaimed. Miller works separately for a private investment firm which may at any time invest in companies whose products are discussed, and no disclosure of securities transactions will be made. Until late 2006, Miller was the Chief Content Officer for Ziff Davis Media, responsible for overseeing the editorial positions of Ziff Davis's magazines, websites, and events. As Editorial Director for Ziff Davis Publishing since 1997, Miller took an active role in helping to identify new editorial needs in the marketplace and in shaping the editorial positioning of every Ziff Davis title. Under Miller's supervision, PC Magazine grew to have the largest readership of any technology publication in the world. PC Magazine evolved from its successful PCMagNet service on CompuServe to become one of the earliest and most successful web sites. As an accomplished journalist, well versed in product testing and evaluating and writing about software issues, and as an experienced public speaker, Miller has become a leading commentator on the computer industry. He has participated as a speaker and panelist in industry conferences, has appeared on numerous business television and radio programs discussing technology issues, and is frequently quoted in major newspapers. His areas of special expertise include the Internet and its applications, desktop productivity tools, and the use of PCs in business applications. Prior to joining PC Magazine, Miller was editor-in-chief of InfoWorld, which he joined as executive editor in 1985. At InfoWorld, he was responsible for development of the magazine's comparative reviews and oversaw the establishment of the InfoWorld Test Center. Previously, he was the west coast bureau chief for Popular Computing, and senior editor for Building Design & Construction. Miller earned a BS in computer science from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in Troy, New York and an MS in journalism from the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois. He has received several awards for his writing and editing, including being named to Medill's Alumni Hall of Achievement

item.title: Obsbot Meet Flip Review: The Ultimate Ultra-Portable 4K Webcam
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.38
It’s a shame Obsbot already used the Tiny name for its gimbal-mounted webcam line, because the $119 Meet Flip is far smaller than any of them. It gives up motorized pan-and-tilt in favor of a matchbook-sized design that can be tossed in any bag or pocket with ease. Its diminutive form belies its excellent performance, capturing bright, sharp 4K video and incredibly clear sound. It easily earns our Editors’ Choice award for the best ultra-portable webcam. Folded up, the Meet Flip measures 0.7 by 1.6 by 1.6 inches (HWD), a fifth the size of the 1.9-by-1.8-by-2.5-inch Tiny SE ($99) and a quarter that of the 2.3-by-1.6-by-1.6-inch Tiny 3 Lite ($199). In fact, with its flat profile dominated by a wide, hinged jaw and a prominent lip for placing it on the top of a laptop or monitor, it looks less like a webcam and more like a clip meant to hold one. It’s the first webcam I’ve seen that’s genuinely small and thin enough to fit into the change pocket of a pair of jeans. The jaw works quite well, with a stiff hinge and rubberized inner panels for gripping the top of your monitor. It helps that the webcam is a featherweight 1.33 ounces compared with the 2.22-ounce Tiny 3 and 2.58-ounce Tiny 3 Lite, letting it perch on the thinnest laptops. The bottom of the jaw also has a screw mount for using a tripod. When it’s not in use, the only hint that the Meet Flip isn’t just a clip for another webcam is the USB-C port on the back. To reveal its true nature, flip up the front module, a minuscule 0.4-by-0.5-by-1.6-inch block holding the camera lens, microphone grille, and indicator LED. It doesn’t come with a carrying case as the pricier Tiny 3 does, but since it doesn’t have a moving gimbal to protect and folds up into such a small, secure package, that’s not a problem. Neither the Tiny SE nor Tiny 3 Lite comes with a case, and while they're hardly flimsy, you still need to keep their freely moving parts in mind when toting them around. All three of the webcams are really small, but for truly simple on-the-go portability without spending $350 on the top-of-the-line Tiny 3 with its case, you’ll probably want to go with the Meet Flip. The Meet Flip isn’t capable of mechanical pan and tilt like the gimbal-equipped Tiny models, but its little camera capsule otherwise shares nearly the same specs as the Tiny 3 Lite. It uses a 48MP Type 1/2 (1/2-inch) CMOS sensor paired with an f/1.8 lens, offering a 79.1-degree field of view in 4:3 and a 72-degree field of view in 16:9. It can record in 4K30 and 1080p60, focus as close as 10 centimeters, and supports a 4x digital zoom. The only thing the Tiny 3 Lite has that it lacks is a 1080p120 slow-motion capture mode. Like Obsbot’s other cameras, you can adjust the settings of and directly control the Meet Flip with the Obsbot Center software. It lets you use both automatic and extensive manual exposure controls, plus a variety of color and beauty retouching filters. It also enables automatic framing of your face via digital zoom, though since the camera is fixed and not on a gimbal, it lacks clever pan-and-tilt options like those on the Tiny 3 and Tiny 3 Lite. It doesn’t support voice control, but you can turn on two hand gestures: holding up your hand to toggle automatic framing and holding up your finger and thumb to toggle digital zoom. As a fun little bonus, Obsbot Center lets you set the Meet Flip to Switch 2 mode, which drops the webcam’s output to 1080p and lets you use it with a Nintendo Switch 2 for GameChat and other video features. For such a tiny camera, the Meet Flip is impressively sharp. 4K30 test video under strong direct lighting is very detailed, showing individual hairs on my head, beard, and eyebrows. With more casual, overhead-only lighting, it still looks quite good with auto-exposure. When there isn’t much light shining directly on the subject, it can benefit from a bit of exposure tweaking. Footage captured in a dark room, with my face lit only by a laptop screen, still shows a fair amount of detail, though it's predictably buried under heavy noise. My beard is softened in the test footage, but the controls of my capture software are visible in the reflection in my glasses. It isn’t nearly as shockingly sharp low-light video as the Tiny 3 Lite's, but you’ll still be recognizable. As with all webcams, the first step to a good picture is good lighting. While it doesn’t have a gimbal like the Tiny series, the Meet Flip follows in the footsteps of its pan-and-tilt siblings with an excellent microphone. Audio in test recordings from laptop distance (about 18 inches away) is impressively clean, with my voice coming through without a hint of fuzziness, room echo, or any noise from my air conditioner. It sounds a bit more distant if you pull further back to monitor distance (24 inches or more), but even with some room echo, it’s very clear. It’s easily one of the best webcam microphones I’ve tested if you can stay fairly close to it, and can be reliably used for both voice calls and casual recording and streaming (though as always, if you’re serious about content creation, you should invest in a dedicated microphone).
