Final Thoughts Obsbot Meet Flip - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Obsbot once again impresses with a webcam that offers great-looking, great-sounding video in a ridiculously small package. If you want a webcam you can bring anywhere without taking up virtually any space in your bag, this is it. The Meet Flip's performance already justifies its price, but its keychain-sized profile really seals it as the best webcam for on-the-go use, and it earns our Editors’ Choice award. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: September's Desktop Deals Bring Powerful PCs at Deep Discounts From Dell, HP, Lenovo, and More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.66
There are lots of different kinds of computers out there, from palm-sized productivity machines to desktop towers. While we do a lot of stuff on a laptop, there's no substitute for a full-bore PC with all of the trimmings, and major manufacturers build and release numerous different models every year. If you're shopping for one, it's a tough time for prices, but deals are out there if you know where to look—and we do. At PCMag, we review desktops more thoroughly than anywhere else, and with over 40 years in the business, our system can't be topped. We evaluate desktops using a transparent system of metrics, factoring in price, features, design, and performance for work and play. We compare capabilities with ever-evolving benchmark tests, as well as run real-world applications and games, to determine the real value of each system and how the deals compare. Best Home and Office Desktop Deals These desktop towers prioritize reliability and value over high-octane gaming performance. Major brands like Dell, HP, and Lenovo specialize in these PCs, which usually cost around $1,000 for worthwhile models. If you have nostalgia for the glory days of wood-paneled computer rooms and the AOL dial-up noise, HP's OmniDesk towers combine vintage aesthetics with current-gen performance in an affordable package. We have a CES preview of this line, where we noted that the wood-grain front panel conceals surprisingly effective cooling fans and tons of ports. The footprint is also relatively small, but a ton of tech is packed inside, so it's not lightweight enough to be considered portable. Inside the case, you get a capable Intel Core Ultra 7 processor that easily tackles everyday productivity and entertainment. RAM and storage are light, but the price is right, as Best Buy has a nice discount on this configuration right now. For a slightly slimmer profile with solid performance, Lenovo's IdeaCentre tower PCs have always been a good option. We don't have a full review of this model, but we were impressed by its 2023 iteration, with top features including a compact chassis, good connectivity, and an install refreshingly free of bloatware. This loadout ships with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265 processor, coupled with 16GB of RAM for smooth operation on most major productivity apps. Port selection is another strong point, with seven USB ports and an HDMI 2.1 output for your monitor of choice. While the integrated Intel UHD graphics aren't cutting-edge, it even works for casual gaming. Best All-In-One Desktop Deals All-in-one desktops pack all of the computing components inside the monitor housing for easier setup and less cable management, and what they lose in customization, they make up for in convenience. We have discounts on a few solid Windows all-in-ones for work and play. We gave an Editors' Choice award to the latest iteration of Dell's all-in-one desktop in our review, commenting that it hit all the marks we expect for a general-purpose home desktop with ease, starting with a cutting-edge Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processor and following it up with plenty of RAM and storage for everyday productivity. The 27-inch FHD screen is touch-enabled, bright, and crisp, with surprisingly assertive stereo speakers. Connectivity is also terrific, with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 along with plenty of ports, although we wish more of them were on the front edge of the screen. The included wireless mouse and keyboard are high quality, and it comes with Windows 11 Pro installed. For a Windows alternative, Lenovo's IdeaCentre has a bigger screen and more onboard storage than the iMac above. We had a mixed but ultimately positive time reviewing this all-in-one. Our reviewer noted that it was well-constructed with lots of ports on multiple sides, and the included wireless keyboard and mouse were comfortable. The 10-core Intel Core i7-13620H processor is suited for everyday productivity, as well as streaming video and surfing the web. Although the FHD screen isn't the highest resolution, it's pleasurable to use for long stretches thanks to an antiglare coating and hardware-based blue light reduction. Snagging this one for under $900 is a fantastic bargain. Best Mini PC Deals Squeezed for space? A mini PC might be the answer. They pack tons of power into cases around the size of a stack of CDs, and are surprisingly capable. We have a Dell compact that's designed for businesses, as well as a creative powerhouse from Kamrui. More mainstream companies also make compact PCs, and this Dell OptiPlex is a solid choice for most productivity-oriented applications. It tackles spreadsheets and presentations with ease, and a plethora of ports let you connect up to four individual monitors in up to 4K resolution (not all at once, of course). It comes with Windows 11 Pro installed and virtually no manufacturer bloatware, so you can have it up and running in minutes. The 14th-generation Intel i3 processor isn't the most impressive chip on the market, but it's capable enough for most everyday office use. Chinese company Kamrui produces a wide range of mini desktop loadouts, and they're impressive from a value proposition, with high-quality components and sturdy design. Amazon has a 19% price cut on the Hyper H2 Mini, which is targeted toward content creators with 32GB of RAM and a full 1TB SSD, along with multi-monitor 4K support thanks to HDMI, USB-C, and DisplayPort outputs. The cooling system is up to the task as well, with centrifugal fans, twin copper heat pipes, and two fin-stack cooling modules. See where it clocks in on our rundown of the best Windows mini PCs. Finally, here's a nicely-priced MSI mini that really gets the job done. You can read our extensive review of the Cubi NUC to see how it performed in our benchmarking tests, but the short version is that it's got a speedy 14-core processor with integrated neural processing unit for Copilot AI, and solid design to work in tight spaces with peak efficiency. Port selection is diverse, with plenty of USB connections on the front and Thunderbolt, HDMI, and a pair of 2.5G Ethernet ports on the back. It even has a corded power button so you can mount it on a wall or in a hard-to-reach spot and still turn it on and off easily. For the money, this is one of the better mini PCs on the market. Best Home and Office Desktop Deals - HP OmniDesk Intel Ultra 7 2TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,374.99 With Code "JULY4PC25" - HP OmniDesk Ryzen 7 RTX 3050 2TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $649.99 ($1,969.99) Save $1,320.00 - Dell Tower Plus Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5060 1TB SSD 16G... — $1,579.99 ($2,129.99) Save $550.00 - Dell Tower Intel Ultra 7 1TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,249.99 ($1,449.99) Save $200.00 - HP All-in-One 27 Ryzen AI 7 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $799.99 ($1,349.99) Save $550.00 - Dell 24 All-in-One Intel i5 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,049.99 ($1,249.99) Save $200.00 - Dell 27 All-in-One Intel 5 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $949.99 ($1,149.99) Save $200.00 Best Gaming Desktop Deals Gaming desktops need high-capability components to be worthwhile, including dedicated GPUs, lots of onboard RAM, and powerful fans to keep it all cool. We've got a few good gaming tower offers right now, notably a pair of battlestations from iBuyPower and HP. HP might not be the first name you think of when it comes to gaming hardware, but its Omen line consistently tests well in the midrange space, with cost-effective builds perfect for 1440p play. We gave an Editors' Choice award to the Omen 35L desktop in our review, noting that it had an ultra-efficient cooling system that kept it running silently even under heavy load, and the easy-access case and industry-standard part selection made it a great pick for upgrading and customizing. The Blackwell-series GeForce 5060 is tuned for medium-resolution performance at fast frame rates, and a full 1TB SSD is beefy enough for your save files. It looks cool, too, with a ceramic white metal case and tempered glass side panels. For an AMD-powered gaming machine that pushes the envelope at a reasonable price, this prebuilt from iBuyPower is worth a look, especially with a $300 price drop from Walmart. We gave the RX 9070XT graphics card an Editors' Choice award in our review, noting that it combined vastly improved ray-tracing performance with great cooling and a reasonable price, competing very capably with Nvidia's current-generation cards. The rest of the silicon loadout is solid for the price, including a speedy Ryzen 9 processor and 32GB of DDR5 RAM for seamless multitasking and content creation. The liquid CPU cooling system and RGB fans keep the whole enterprise stable under pressure. Walmart is really bringing the smoke this week with gaming desktop deals, and snagging a potent performer like MSI's Codex Z2 with the new RTX 5070 Ti at a $500 price drop is worth the final spot on our list. Running off of the Ryzen 7 8700F processor, it's absolutely fast enough to handle all of today's latest games, and the GPU and RAM combination will give you fast framerates at 1440p and even stretch into 4K for aspirational resolution hounds looking to overclock a bit. The chassis is a cool piece of tech as well, with attractive RGB lighting and well-designed airflow, although the fans can run a bit loud. Best Gaming Desktop Deals - HP Omen 35L Intel Ultra 9 RTX 5080 2TB SSD 64GB RAM Desktop — $4,699.99 ($6,499.99) Save $1,800.00 - HP Omen 45L Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5070 1TB SSD Desktop — $2,699.99 ($3,599.99) Save $900.00 - Alienware Aurora Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5060 Ti 1TB SSD... — $2,149.99 ($2,459.99) Save $310.00 - Alienware Area-51 Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5080 1TB SSD 3... — $3,899.99 ($4,299.99) Save $400.00 - Alienware Area-51 Intel Ultra 9 RTX 5090 2TB SSD 3... — $5,999.99 ($6,199.99) Save $200.00 - HP Omen 16L Ryzen 7 RTX 5060 1TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,012.49 With Code "BACK2SCHOOL25" How Much Should I Pay for a Desktop Computer? Your money goes further with desktop PCs and their components than with laptops. You can find complete mini PCs for less than $400 and perfectly serviceable small towers for $500 to $600. Gaming desktops with dedicated graphics cards start at around $700. You can also find all-in-one (AIO) desktops, with the display and all of the computing components built into a single device, starting at around $600. The sky's the limit once you get into high-end gaming PCs and business-workstation power desktops, but the prices above are in the right range for most mainstream buyers. How Much Does a Good Budget PC Cost? Expect to pay at least $500 for a basic, competent small tower for day-in/day-out productivity and web work. You'll find plenty of models for less than $500, especially in the mini PC class, but you should insist on at least 8GB of system memory for any PC, with 16GB required at minimum for AI tasks. For anything beyond basic productivity work, look for an Intel Core i5 (or Ultra 5) or AMD Ryzen 5 processor at least. Which Brands Offer the Best Desktop Discounts? Some brands post deals and discounts on their products more often than others, particularly Acer. Dell, HP, and Lenovo also do this, but you should always double-check exactly what you're getting and whether you can buy it for less at other retailers. Brands like Lenovo adjust their prices frequently, making assessing the raw value of deals you see there difficult. Notably, Apple has improved its image as a value-focused brand, permanently dropping prices on some of its laptops and often hosting limited deals on shopping holidays. What Is the Best Desktop Under $800? Our experts have named the Acer Aspire TC-1775-UR11 their top budget pick for, "packing a 14th Gen Core i7 processor, Wi-Fi 6E, USB-C, and a compact design that tucks under your desk." We've seen this model go for as low as $557 on Amazon. For more budget options, check out our top picks for the best cheap desktop PCs. What Is the Best Gaming Desktop Under $1,000? Finding a really good model under a grand is a big ask. Your best bet is going to be the Asus TUF Gaming T500, which pairs a mobile processor with a discrete graphics card inside a small-footprint desktop. Our experts said, "This cute, efficient rig excels for 1080p gaming, but its CPU, motherboard, power supply, and cooling scheme limit its future upgradability." Right now it's going for around $959.99 at Best Buy. About Our Experts K. Thor Jensen is a writer and cartoonist living in the Pacific Northwest. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. After starting my career at PCMag as an intern more than a decade ago, I’m back as one of its editors, focused on managing laptops, desktops, and components coverage. With 15 years of experience, I have been on staff and published in technology review publications, including PCMag (of course!), Laptop Magazine, Tom’s Guide, TechRadar, and IGN. Along the way, I’ve tested and reviewed hundreds of laptops and helped develop testing protocols. I have expertise in testing all forms of laptops and desktops using the latest tools. I’m also well-versed in video game hardware and software coverage. When she isn't perusing online stores for deals, Jade enjoys playing video games (mostly JRPGs and roguelikes), sorting board game components neatly into containers, and building Gundam models. Her love of electronics has persisted through her youth and has resulted in a collection of gaming peripherals including keyboards and controllers, scale figures, and art work. Jade lives in blissful harmony with her wife, cat, and two chinchillas—as well as a host of houseplants.

item.title: I’ve Tested Hundreds of Cameras: Here Are My 10 Best Pro Photography Tips
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.51
Are you ready to step up your photography to the next level? Regardless of whether you're just starting out with a camera or if you've been taking snapshots for years, there's always room to learn and grow as a creator. I've reviewed cameras at PCMag for 15 years and have taken countless photos in that time. That's let me try out different techniques, learn from my mistakes, and really get to know how to squeeze the best results out of the newest gear—read on for some of the best tips and tricks that I've learned along the way. 1. Learn to Process Raw Images Digital cameras are set up to record images in an 8-bit JPG format out of the box. These pictures are "developed" from the sensor by your camera's image processor and leave little headroom to adjust exposure or color balance. They also suffer from lossy noise reduction and compression. Almost all interchangeable lens cameras and many advanced compacts support a Raw format, either with 12-bit or 14-bit color sampling. The extra data lets you open shadows to save poorly exposed backlit shots, or apply an artistic color grade to a photo without losing any picture quality. Raw photos aren't meant to be shared right out of the camera, however, so it's up to you to learn how to process them. You'll need software to do so, but you can start out with the software that came with your PC (Microsoft Photos) or Mac (Apple Photos) to handle the basics. If you like the creative freedom you get with these apps, consider upgrading to a professional workflow application with more features like Adobe Lightroom, Capture One, or Skylum Luminar. The Best Raw Processors We've Tested One more thing: If you're nervous about using Raw format, don't fret. Your camera almost certainly has a Raw+JPG setting that will save each picture in both file types. This takes up more space on your memory card, but is a useful safety net. 2. Move Your Flash Off Camera Most serious cameras omit an in-body flash, so chances are you'll end up shopping for an add-on flash soon. On-camera flash is good for filling in shadows when taking portraits outdoors on a sunny day, and more powerful flashguns like the Godox V1 can brighten dimly lit interiors. With flash, the direction of the light is as important as its power. At minimum, you should get a flash that lets you point its light up, back, or to the side to bounce off of a wall. This will give you softer, more diffused light and help avoid the harsh look of direct flash. But if you want to get fancy, pick up a flash that works with a wireless transmitter. I use Godox R2 TTL transmitters with my cameras and have found them reliable, versatile, and more affordable than high-end options from industry leader Profoto. With an R2 transmitter on my camera, I can simultaneously trigger multiple off-camera strobes with manual or automatic Through the Lens (TTL) power to light a scene. The Best Off-Camera Lights We've Tested I prefer Godox over a first-party solution simply because I can use one set of lights for several brands of cameras. If you end up switching camera brands later on it's just a matter of switching transmitters, not replacing your entire lighting kit. One note, Godox R2 TTL flashes are also sold under other brand names, and are thankfully cross-compatible. I've reviewed several some Godox lights sold under the Flashpoint brand and they work together seamlessly. 3. Try Some Weird Lenses Chances are you've already moved away from your 18-55mm kit lens, either opting for a better quality zoom or a fast prime lens. But if you're stuck in a creative rut, or just want to experiment with some new types of photography, a specialized lens can really come in handy. You can opt for a super-sharp macro lens that can focus close and fill your frame with small objects. You can also go in the opposite direction and experiment with Lensbaby, a creative lens system that allows you to adjust the plane of focus. They let you create photos that have a sharp point of focus that gives way to soft, swirly dreaminess. My Favorite Artsy Lenses If you have a mirrorless camera your choices are even more vast. Numerous lens adapters are available that allow you to mount virtually any lens to these cameras for use in manual focus mode. I love using antique lenses with cameras simply because of their character and value. Check out How to Use Vintage Lenses on Mirrorless Cameras for more ideas. If you want to try a lens before you buy, you can rent online from Lensrentals. 4. Clean Your Image Sensor Sensor dust. If you use a mirrorless camera, you're likely familiar, as it's far easier to get a few specks of detritus on your image sensor versus an SLR, simply because there is no mirror to protect it, so the sensor is exposed when you swap lenses. Some good practices can help reduce the chance of dust getting onto the sensor. First, make sure the camera is turned off when you change lenses as dust is more prone to stick on a powered, electrified sensor. Some newer, pro-level mirrorless cameras include a shield that protects the sensor when powered down, but most do not, so you should also try to avoid changing lenses outdoors in rough weather. But even if you're the most careful, meticulous photographer in the world, you will end up with dust on your image sensor at some point. You might not notice if you use your lenses at wide apertures, but the spots are apparent at smaller f-stops. Many mirrorless cameras include automatic dust reduction systems that vibrate the sensor to shake smaller particles away, but they're not foolproof. If you have a dust spot that won't go away, blowing it off with an air puffer typically works. For more persistent spots, consider a cleaning kit from Visible Dust and Lenspen or, if you aren't comfortable doing it yourself, a professional cleaning is in order. 5. Throw Away the Bundled Neck Strap If you're going to carry your camera around all day, you should do it in comfort. Most mirrorless cameras come with a basic nylon strap without any padding. Even worse, the strap is typically covered with brand logos, so you turn into a walking advertisement, and it attaches using a confounding set of loops and grommets. I've been taking pictures for decades, and I still haven't figured out how to properly secure them. Third-party straps come in all shapes and sizes, so you've got freedom to choose between different styles. Some photographers swear by wrist straps; others may prefer a cross-body sling to support telephoto lenses. My favorite is the Peak Design Slide Lite, which is comfortable to wear cross-body and attaches to your camera with a simple loop and anchor. Sling straps, like those from BlackRapid, are often used by event photographers who carry multiple bodies with heavy lenses attached. They're a good match if you have a telephoto lens with its own tripod collar, too. I still reach for one when using a big zoom lens. You can also go the classic route with a wide, fabric strap—readily available via Etsy shops, or go full hipster with an artisanal, handcrafted leather strap like those made in Brooklyn by Tap & Dye. 6. Get a Tripod, Monopod, or Gimbal There are some scenes where holding the camera in your hand doesn't make the most sense. If you are interested in taking pictures of landscapes, cityscapes, or architecture, a tripod is a handy tool for careful, deliberate composition. A tripod isn't your only option for camera support. Sports and wildlife photogs who use big lenses and need to move around frequently are better off with a single leg, a monopod, to give arm muscles a rest without sacrificing freedom of movement. And if you're more interested in video, consider getting a powered gimbal for smooth handheld footage. Tripods I Recommend Lightweight options like the Peak Design Travel Tripod sacrifice some stability and features in favor of size, but are a great option if you spend more time at airports than at home. Photographers who use heavy telephoto lenses or medium-format gear will want something beefier. If you haven't shopped for a tripod before, it's worth reading my buying guide to help you decide how much to spend and what type to target for your gear and photo interests. 7. Experiment With New Techniques If you find yourself in a creative rut, or simply bored with the images you're taking, take it as a sign to move outside your comfort zone. You can make so many types of images with your camera, so try something new if you're looking for a new challenge. My first advice is to try different shutter speeds. You can use long exposures (1/4-second or longer) to smooth out flowing water or to add motion blur to moving subjects. If you want to bend time even further, check if your camera has a time-lapse capture mode. You can also try different angles or scenes. If you usually take landscapes outdoors, consider adding a telephoto for wildlife opportunities. If you often use a macro lens to hone on on the little details, switch over to a wide angle. You should expect some growing pains when trying something new, and perhaps a memory card of images that aren't up to your usual standards, but missed photos are a part of improving your craft. 8. Fly a Drone You don't have to just take images when standing on level ground. Adding a drone to your toolkit makes it possible to grab shots from perspectives you'd never be able to get otherwise. Most drones can capture 4K video and Raw format images, and current models are safe to fly (assuming you follow the rules). Check out our top picks in the category. The Best Drones for Photographers 9. Print Your Work It's easy to share your photos online or view them on a digital picture frame, but if you take a photo you truly love, it deserves to be printed. You can print at home on an inkjet, but for the best results, you'll want to go with a dedicated printing service. Many of our favorite photo printing services offer fun ways to display your work, including prints on canvas, metallic paper, and true black and white photo paper for a classic look. You can also opt for a custom photo book, an update on the classic family album with your photos printed directly onto the pages. The Best Photo Printing Services We've Tried 10. Upgrade Your Camera for the Right Reasons If you're enthusiastic about your photos, you might be itching to buy a new camera. There are plenty of reasons to upgrade, but you don't always have to have the latest camera to take good photos. That said, most newer mirrorless cameras include far better autofocus systems and video features versus older DSLRs, so there are good reasons to get a new camera. Before you spend money, ask yourself, "What frustrates me about my current camera?" and make sure a replacement addresses your gripes head-on. The Best Cameras We've Tested For more inspiration and guidance, check out our explainers on photographing lightning and fireworks. If you're looking for a new camera or lens, be sure to peruse our digital cameras product guide for the latest reviews, and our roundup of the best digital cameras for the top products we've tested. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: HP OmniBook Ultra 14 (2026) Review: A Top-Tier Ultraportable With Good Looks, Better Power
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.23
We're in a golden age for luxe ultraportables, which makes it seriously challenging to stand out in this increasingly crowded segment. HP's OmniBook Ultra 14 does just that. From its sleek aluminum chassis and vibrant OLED display to its excellent webcam, impressive speakers, and all-day battery life, nearly every aspect of this 14-incher feels carefully considered. Though the OmniBook Ultra 14 is undeniably pricey, starting at $1,799.99 and reaching $4,049.99 as tested, it delivers exactly the kind of experience that power users expect in this elite tier. Alongside rivals like Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell's XPS 14, the OmniBook Ultra 14 earns its place among the best premium ultraportables available today, earning an Editors' Choice award alongside the best of its kind. HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 brings Intel’s latest "Panther Lake" silicon to the premium ultraportable market. Every configuration is built around a 16-core Core Ultra Series 3 processor, starting with the Core Ultra 7 356H and scaling to the flagship Core Ultra X9 388H featured in our test unit. Systems equipped with the Core Ultra X7 and X9 house Intel's highly capable Arc B390 integrated graphics. The memory and storage options are also impressive. You can configure the system with up to 64GB of LPDDR5X memory running at 9,600 megatransfers per second and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 SSD, though the highest RAM allotment is reserved for configurations with the Core Ultra X9 chip. Those specs make the OmniBook Ultra 14 a good fit for demanding multitasking and content-creation workloads. Naturally, the premium components come at a cost, and the ongoing component shortages don't help much. With prices ranging from $1,799.99 to more than $4,000 for my test machine, the OmniBook Ultra 14 competes directly with flagship machines like Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell’s XPS 14. Offered in Eclipse Gray or the Silk Sand colorway of our review unit (the Sand shade is an extra $20), the OmniBook Ultra 14 looks every bit the flagship. Its all-aluminum chassis feels exceptionally rigid, with virtually no flex in the lid or keyboard deck. The laptop even passed MIL-STD durability testing. Then you get subtle touches—machined edges, a responsive haptic touchpad, and understated reflective logos—that elevate the overall experience. At just 0.42 inches thick and 2.81 pounds, the OmniBook is exceptionally sleek and remarkably easy to carry, undercutting Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro in both measurements. The only major drawback is connectivity: HP has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and a headphone jack, but omits USB-A altogether, which can be frustrating if you're juggling older peripherals. Even so, the system boasts a bunch of modern conveniences that help make up for the missing ports: Wi-Fi 7, a super-sharp 5MP webcam with privacy shutter, and a compact GaN wall charger. HP covers the system with a one-year warranty, with multiyear extensions and accidental damage coverage available. In our testing, the OmniBook Ultra 14 offered up a premium experience, with a lot of strong points that worked together brilliantly. From its design to its input devices and everything in between, the system feels thoughtfully executed. The 3K (2,880-by-1,800-pixel) display makes for one of the system’s leading features—this is the type of screen that you’ll think about long after you’ve seen it. Sharp detail, rich color, and punchy contrast bring any content to life, with touch input and a smooth 120Hz refresh rate augmenting everyday practicality. It pairs well with the quad-speaker system, which sounds closer to a small Bluetooth speaker than a typical laptop. HP's webcam also impresses, offering a crisp, well-exposed picture that outclasses the usual laptop fare. The laptop's input devices are just as impressive. The lattice-free keyboard design looks clean, and the sloped key edges help preserve a sense of spacing. You also get nice key travel and a quiet, cushioned feel. I also appreciated the status LEDs integrated into the mute, microphone, function lock, and power keys, which make it easy to confirm key system states at a glance. The white key backlighting could stand out a bit more under ordinary lighting conditions, but it'll do in the dark. The system gets another usability boost from effective thermal management. The laptop runs quietly day to day and stays comfortable to the touch under heavier workloads. Though the lack of USB-C ports might force you to pack some adapters, the OmniBook Ultra 14 remains a polished, dependable premium ultraportable that nails the core experience. I tested HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 in a flagship configuration featuring Intel’s Core Ultra X9 388H (16 cores, 5.1GHz turbo), Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics, 64GB of LPDDR5X-9600 memory, and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 solid-state drive. The system runs Windows 11 Pro and represents the most powerful version of the OmniBook Ultra 14 currently available. To see how well that hardware translates into real-world performance, we compared the OmniBook to similarly upscale systems, including Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro ($2,349), the Asus ExpertBook Ultra ($3,599.99 as tested), the Dell XPS 14 ($2,199.99), and the Framework Laptop 13 Pro ($2,932). All of those models target power users seeking a premium experience. While the OmniBook’s Core Ultra X9 388H sits at the top of Intel’s lineup, it delivers only a marginal edge over the Core Ultra X7 358H silicon its competitors use: a higher boost clock of 5.1GHz versus 4.8GHz. The more illuminating comparison will be against Apple's 10-core M5 chip. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The OmniBook Ultra 14 delivered consistently strong productivity results. Its 9,736-point showing in PCMark 10 ranks among the best we've seen from any laptop, trailing only the ExpertBook Ultra by a narrow margin. The OmniBook also impressed us with its storage performance, as HP’s PCIe 5.0 SSD delivered a top-tier score. The OmniBook came down to Earth in our CPU-focused tests, proving itself competitive rather than class-leading. It traded blows with the ExpertBook Ultra, XPS 14, and Framework Laptop 13 Pro, notably excelling in Handbrake while falling slightly behind in Cinebench multi-core testing. These results are hardly surprising, given the Core Ultra X9 388H's modest clock-speed advantage over its competitors' Core Ultra X7 processors. Apple’s M5-powered MacBook Pro proved to be the system to beat, though its performance advantages aren’t large enough to diminish HP’s excellent overall results. We challenge all systems' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. Intel's Arc B390 integrated GPU doesn't transform the OmniBook Ultra 14 outright into a great gaming laptop, though we've seen how the Arc B390, in other tests, is more than up to the task of casual gaming. (That's largely beside the point with any premium ultraportable, of course.) However, the silicon kept the laptop competitive with the rest of the pack, delivering strong results throughout our graphics testing. The XPS 14, ExpertBook Ultra, and Laptop 13 Pro performed similarly, which you'd expect considering that they also rely on the Arc B390 in the configurations we tested. Apple’s MacBook Pro remained formidable, but the OmniBook nosed ahead of it in two out of the three tests the MacBook was compatible with. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). It’s tough to fault the OmniBook Ultra 14’s battery life, which should comfortably power through a cross-country flight or a full day off the outlet. If you want to quibble, several of its rivals showed the same outstanding stamina. HP's OLED display also deserves praise. While it didn't match the searing brightness of the ExpertBook Ultra or Framework Laptop 13 Pro, HP still chose well. Its sharp resolution, near-complete DCI-P3 color coverage, and high brightness offer the premium viewing experience expected at this price. While brighter screens are available, few people will walk away disappointed by this panel. Final Thoughts HP OmniBook Ultra 14 (2026) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Few laptops feel as complete as the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. Its premium design, OLED screen, excellent webcam and speakers, strong performance, and long battery life make this a compelling package that’s worthy of its flagship status. Naturally, it's priced to match, but no more so than rivals like Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro. Its balance of style, refinement, and everyday usability earns it an easy Editors' Choice recommendation as one of the finest premium Windows ultraportables. About Our Expert Computers are my lifelong obsession. I wrote my first laptop review in 2005 for NotebookReview.com, continued with a consistent PC-reviewing gig at Computer Shopper in 2014, and moved to PCMag in 2018. Here, I test and review the latest high-performance laptops and desktops, and sometimes a key core PC component or two. I also review enterprise computing solutions for StorageReview. I work full-time as a technical analyst for a business software and services company. My hobbies are digital photography, fitness, two-stroke engines, and reading. I’m a graduate of the Rochester Institute of Technology.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: To Upgrade or Not?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.16
Table of Contents Not everything at Apple's Surprise and Shine event was about the foldable iPhone Duo. There's plenty to be excited about with the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, especially if you're moving up from an older model. The two new iPhones differ very little from each other, aside from screen size and battery life. More importantly, they're pretty similar to last year's iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, which remain strong performers but are no longer available in the Apple Store (though you could save money by buying back stock or second-hand). We've spent some time with the 18 Pro and Pro Max and have extensively tested the iPhone 17 Pro line. Here's how to decide if the upgrade to 18 Pro is worth it for you. Full Specs | Apple iPhone 17 Pro | Apple iPhone 18 Pro | | |---|---|---| | Operating System | | | | Operating System | iOS 26 | iOS 27 | | CPU | | | | CPU | Apple A19 Pro | Apple A20 Pro | | Dimensions | | | | Dimensions | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | | Screen Size | | | | Screen Size | 6.3 inches | 6.3 inches | | Screen Resolution | | | | Screen Resolution | 2,622 by 1,206 pixels | 2622 by 1206 pixels | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | | | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP; 18MP | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP, 25MP | | Battery Life (As Tested) | | | | Battery Life (As Tested) | 27 hours, 42 minutes | TBD | Pricing: Increases Across the Board The iPhone 18 Pro lineup spans two models and various storage capacities. This is the first year that Apple is offering 2TB of storage with the smaller iPhone 18 Pro. Here's how it all breaks down: - iPhone 18 Pro: 256GB, $1,199; 512GB, $1,399; 1TB, $1,599; 2TB, $1,999 - iPhone 18 Pro Max: 256GB, $1,299; 512GB, $1,499; 1TB, $1,899; 2TB, $2,499 For comparison, here is last year's original pricing for the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max from when they debuted: - iPhone 17 Pro: 256GB, $1,099; 512GB, $1,299; 1TB, $1,499 - iPhone 17 Pro Max: 256GB, $1,199; 512GB, $1,399; 1TB, $1,599; 2TB, $1,999 In short, pricing is up $100 across the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, thanks to all the component shenanigans happening globally in the supply chain. At the very least, if you want to spring for 2TB of storage, it's available on the smaller phone now. Winner: iPhone 17 Pro Design: Out With the Orange and In With the New There was nothing wrong with last year's iPhone 17 Pro redesign of the rear-shaped camera island, and it was clearly popular, as I see the orange phone in many hands. But the iPhone 18 Pro's colorways are simply outstanding compared with last year's offerings. Last year's special colors were Cosmic Orange and Deep Blue, but this year's are Glacier, an ice blue, and Burgundy, a wine red. Deep Black and Silver are also available for those who prefer something more conventional. Sizing hasn't changed between generations. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro are both 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches (HWD). The iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone 17 Pro Max are both 6.43 by 3.07 by 0.34 inches. If you want the lightest phone, it's last gen's iPhone 17 Pro at 7.27 ounces. The iPhone 18 Pro bumps the weight up to 7.44 ounces, perhaps due to a reconfiguration of the internal vapor chamber. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the biggest honker of the four devices, and it's half an ounce heavier than last year's iPhone 17 Pro Max. It went from 8.22 ounces to 8.78 ounces. All iPhones share an IP68 water and dust rating. They all have an Action Button, Camera Control, MagSafe, wireless charging, and a USB-C port. Winner: Tie, but iPhone 17 Pro on weight alone Display: Nothing Different to See Here The new iPhone's display is the same as last year's. The iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max feature 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch Super Retina XDR LTPO OLED displays, respectively. It's the same configuration for this year's iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, down to the Ceramic Shield 2 glass for protection. The Dynamic Island also makes its triumphant return this time with support for three live activities at a time. Both last year's and this year's iPhone Pro models feature screens with a pixel density of 460 pixels per inch, an always-on display, and a slightly anti-reflective coating. Peak brightness is still about 3000 nits. Winner: Tie Hardware: First 2nm Process The iPhone 18 Pro features the new Apple A20 Pro built on a 2nm architecture. It's a six-core CPU with two performance cores and four efficiency cores, designed to handle most low-latency AI tasks. Apple began reworking its internal vapor-chamber cooling system with the iPhone 17 Pro, but the iPhone 18 Pro is the model that showcases what's been achieved. It'll be interesting to see how much that helps with performance numbers compared with the A19 Pro, but it's sure to be faster. The iPhone 18 Pro retains USB 3 transfer speeds up to 10Gbps, enabling high-res ProRAW recording to external drives. The internal LIDAR scanner introduced in the 17 Pro series remains a Pro-exclusive feature and is critical for low light, focusing, and spatial room scanning. For connectivity, the iPhone 18 Pro supports sub-6GHz and the fastest form of 5G, mmWave. Apple's custom C2 cellular modem enables this, promising faster uploads and 15% less battery drain while keeping you fully connected to 5G towers—but only the iPhone 18 Pro has it, not the Pro Max. Apple ditched the physical SIM on last year's iPhones. This year's Pro line supports up to two active SIMs simultaneously and eight or more profiles, matching the iPhone 17 Pro. Winner: iPhone 18 Pro Cameras: Variable Aperture Enters the Fold On the spec sheet, you'll see that the iPhone 17 Pro series and the iPhone 18 Pro series have similar camera sensors, at least in megapixels: a rear-facing triple 48MP array. But they differ in one key way: the iPhone 18 Pro is the only one with a variable aperture (ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, ƒ/4.0). It has a secondary 48MP Ultra Wide with the same 120-degree field of view as last year, plus a 48MP telephoto lens with an f/2.8 aperture and 4x optical zoom. An upgrade, but one with a few limitations. The iPhone 18 Pro series also offers native manual Pro controls, letting you adjust not only the aperture but also shutter speed, white balance, and follow with an on-screen exposure histogram. The Pro line can shoot video at up to 4K resolution at 120fps. The front-facing camera stays largely the same. Both generations have an 18MP Center Stage front camera that can shoot 4K video at 60fps. You'll have to wait for our reviews to see whether the variable aperture makes a big difference. But the Pro line is currently the best Apple camera you can get in your pocket. Winner: iPhone 18 Pro Battery Life: We're Going Long Apple doesn't typically detail the battery capacities of its new iPhones. But it did provide projected battery life. The iPhone 18 Pro can play video for up to 36 hours, about a three-hour increase over the 17 Pro's original figure. The iPhone 18 Pro Max lasts up to 45 hours of video playback, which is about a six-hour increase over last year's kit. We'll test battery life to the fullest once we get the devices for review, and we expect them to surpass last year's iPhone 17 Pro series. The projected charging time has also shortened this round. Apple projects 15 minutes to 50% battery with a 60W or higher power adapter. It should reach a full charge in 50 to 55 minutes and can deliver up to six hours of video playback after a five-minute charge. Wireless charging speeds were also increased to support 35W. Both models support MagSafe, Qi2, and Qi wireless charging. Winner: Too Soon to Tell (But Likely the iPhone 18 Pro) Which iPhone Pro is Right For You? It's too early to declare a winner, but the latest iPhone Pro consistently delivers the best performance and point-and-shoot camera capabilities the company offers. However, you don't always need the brand-new newness. For now, here are a couple of things to consider: - If you want the lightest, smallest Pro phone, it's the iPhone 18 Pro. - If you want the best camera capabilities possible, you can't go wrong with either size of the iPhone 18 Pro. - If it's endurance you want, the bigger iPhone 18 Pro Max has a larger battery to accommodate the larger screen, so it will be the one to carry you far. The new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are available for preorder starting Sept. 12. Both phones hit stores on Sept. 18. We will be updating this piece with our full assessment after we lab test the iPhone 18 Pro phones in the coming weeks.

item.title: Best mini PC deals: Top Intel and AMD picks for performance, gaming, and more
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.32
At a glance Top AMD mini PC deal picks - GMKtec M7 Ultra—$750 (12% off on Amazon) - Reatan A8—$519 with coupon (19% off on Amazon with coupon) - Bosgame E5—$260 (11% off on Amazon) Top Intel mini PC deal picks - ACEMAGIC K1—$440 (24% off on Amazon) - Beelink Mini S12 Pro—$369 (14% off on Amazon) - GMKtec G3 Pro—$330 (28% off on Amazon) Whether you’re looking for a productivity mini PC, something for gaming, or just a budget-friendly machine with a small footprint, we’ve got you covered. The team at PCWorld continually sorts through all of the daily mini PC sales and puts together a curated list of the best deals available. Finding the right deals can be tricky, however, because there are so many things to consider, from the configuration to the price. Fear not! I’ve been covering mini PC deals for a long time—and PCWorld has tested thousands of PCs over four decades—so let me help you out. I select our favorite deals by thoroughly examining the list of specs, overall design, user feedback, and general value. The RAM, SSD, and CPU all matter significantly in mini PCs, and if you’re not careful, you may select a “bare-bones” rig that makes you bring your own memory and storage. All of the picks below are hand-selected for not only their performance, but most importantly, their value. I’ve also included some helpful answers to common questions about buying a computer at the bottom of this article. If you’re considering a laptop instead, be sure to check out our best laptop deals, or for more desktop choices check out best computer deals roundup instead—each are updated daily. Updated September 13, 2026 to reflect the latest deals and pricing. Best deals on AMD mini PCs GMKtec M7 Ultra, Ryzen 7 Pro 6850U/Radeon 680M/32GB RAM/1TB SSD/Oculink/quad 4K support—$750 (12% off on Amazon) The GMKtec M7 Ultra for $100 off on Amazon is a strong mini PC for work and light gaming. Its Ryzen 7 Pro 6850U and Radeon 680M graphics provide plenty of power for demanding productivity tasks and less intensive games. You also get a great value thanks to the 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a generous 1TB of onboard SSD storage. The bonus here is the Oculink port, which lets you connect an external graphics card for more serious gaming. Dual 2.5Gb Ethernet ports and two USB4 ports round out this well-equipped machine. Reatan A8, Ryzen 7 8745HS/Radeon 780M/16GB DDR5 RAM/1TB SSD/Oculink/quad 4K support—$519 with coupon (19% off on Amazon with coupon) The Reatan A8 for $120 off with a coupon on Amazon is a great deal on a powerful AMD mini PC. The Ryzen 7 8745HS and Radeon 780M integrated graphics provide plenty of performance for everyday productivity and are capable of light gaming as well. You’re also getting 16GB of DDR5 RAM and a generous 1TB of onboard SSD storage, which is excellent for the price. The addition of an Oculink port is the kicker, allowing you to connect an external graphics card and turn this compact PC into a much more capable gaming machine. Bosgame E5, Ryzen 3 5300U/16GB RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$260 (11% off on Amazon) The Bosgame E5 for $33 off is a great AMD-powered budget option this week. Its Ryzen 3 5300U has enough muscle for everyday work, web browsing, streaming, and general multitasking, while the 16GB of DDR4 RAM should help keep things running smoothly. You also get a 512GB SSD, which is plenty of storage for a basic home or office PC. Triple-4K display support and dual LAN ports are nice extras too, giving this compact desktop a bit more flexibility than its low price suggests. Acemagic K1, Ryzen 7 7730U/16GB RAM/1TB SSD/triple 4K support—$470 (30% off on Amazon) Amazon is offering the Acemagic K1 for $199 off right now, making it a solid option for anyone looking for an affordable everyday PC. The Ryzen 7 7730U is a good productivity processor that should have no trouble with all of your typical browsing or work activities. Plus, 16GB of RAM is plenty for everyday use and the generous 1TB SSD gives you ample room for apps and files. It’s a straightforward mini PC without a lot of flashy extras, but the combination of strong everyday performance and plenty of storage makes it a good value at this price. Getorli Mini PC, Ryzen 5 6600H/16GB LPDDR5 RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$350 (10% off on Amazon) If you’re looking for something a bit more budget-friendly, this Getorli Mini PC for $40 off on Amazon is worth a look. The Ryzen 5 6600H is still a capable processor for productivity and everyday use, and it’s paired with a speedy 16GB of LPDDR5 memory. The 512GB SSD isn’t huge, but it should be enough for most people who mainly need a compact office or home PC. You also get Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3, and triple-display support, making this an affordable option for a multi-monitor workstation. Getorli isn’t a well known name like some of the others on this list, but it’s mini PCs have solid reviews and they are steadily gaining a following due to their great budget-friendly prices. Acemagic Mini PC, Ryzen R2544/16GB RAM/256GB SSD/triple 4K support—$350 (24% off on Amazon with coupon) If you need a compact everyday computer, this Acemagic Mini PC for $110 off on Amazon is another option worth considering. Its Ryzen R2544 processor—a lesser known, powerful budget CPU—and 16GB of DDR4 RAM can handle web browsing, productivity apps, and general office work. The 256GB SSD is a bit small, but it should be enough if you’re willing to store most of your files in the cloud or on an external drive. It also supports up to three 4K displays, making it an inexpensive option for a multi-monitor entertainment machine. Best deals on Intel mini PCs ACEMAGIC K1, Core i5-12600H/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$440 (24% off on Amazon) My favorite Intel-powered mini PC deal right now is the ACEMAGIC K1 for $139 off on Amazon. The Core i5-12600H is a modern, capable processor that should have no trouble handling demanding productivity and multitasking work. Plus, the 16GB of DDR4 RAM gives you enough memory to keep plenty of apps running smoothly. You also get a suitable 512GB of onboard SSD storage and Windows 11 Pro out of the box. At under $500, this is an excellent option with strong performance features in a compact design. Beelink Mini S12 Pro, Intel N100/16GB DDR4 RAM/500GB SSD/dual 4K support—$369 (14% off on Amazon) The Beelink Mini S12 Pro is $70 off on Amazon, making this compact PC a decent pick for basic everyday use. Its Intel N100 processor is modest, but it has more than enough power for web browsing, streaming, office apps, and other light tasks. You also get 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 500GB SSD, so there’s plenty of memory and storage for a budget machine. Throw in Wi-Fi 6, dual 4K display support, and low power consumption, and you’ve got a capable little desktop for home or office use. GMKtec G3 Pro, Core i3-10110U/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/dual 4K support—$330 (28% off on Amazon) At $130 off on Amazon, the GMKtec G3 Pro is a solid budget mini PC for everyday tasks. Admittedly, its Core i3-10110U is getting a little long in the tooth, but it still has enough power for web browsing, office work, streaming, and other light productivity. You also get 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 512GB SSD, which is a decent setup for the price. Dual 4K display support, Wi-Fi 6, and 2.5Gb Ethernet add surprisingly nice connectivity at this price point as well. GMKtec Mini PC, Core i7-1185G7/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$470 (27% off on Amazon) At $180 off on Amazon, this GMKtec Mini PC is worth a look if you want an affordable Intel system with plenty of connectivity. The Core i7-1185G7 is getting a little long in the tooth, but it still has enough muscle for everyday productivity, multitasking, and general home or office use. It comes with 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 512GB SSD, which is a sensible (and affordable) setup for most people. You also get an unusually good selection of ports and networking options, including USB4, 2.5Gb Ethernet, HDMI, DisplayPort, and Wi-Fi 6. Mini PC deals FAQ What should you look for when buying a mini PC? The first thing you have to check off your list is just what configuration you need to get your job done. Are you going to use your new mini PC for browsing only? Then a cheap budget-friendly device with a decent CPU and 16GB of RAM will do the trick. Do you want it to be able to juggle a bunch of apps and not choke on 50 browser tabs? Then a more powerful CPU and at least 32GB of RAM would be better. Do you want to do some light gaming in your downtime? Look for a device that comes with a GPU or Occulink connectivity to hook up an external GPU instead. Are you looking to utilize the mini PC as a home server? Your priority then should be a large SSD—2TB or more. There are devices for each and every one of these scenarios, and they’re all quite affordable. The best part is that mini PCs are… well, small, so they can be placed practically anywhere depending on your intended use and available space. They also support multiple monitors out of the box, which makes it easy to replace your old, larger desktop and you won’t even need to pay for extra hubs. Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer? For most people, the answer is “yes”! Mini PCs are definitely powerful enough to replace desktops for most users, especially if you’re going to use it for work, browsing, or streaming movies. If you want something for photo and video editing, or even gaming, there are models that allow you to do that, but they’ll cost a bit more. If you’re into hardcore gaming, however, you’re still better off with a proper gaming PC or laptop. Can a mini PC run modern games? Mostly, yes. But it will ultimately depend upon the mini PC you buy and which modern games you want to play. Some high-performance mini PCs can run modern AAA games. You might not be able to run them at the highest settings though, and performance will depend heavily on the specific hardware. If you do want to game on a mini PC, look for powerful models with dedicated discrete GPUs such as an Nvidia RTX or AMD Radeon rather than integrated graphics. Alternatively, you can opt for cloud streaming services to game on less powerful mini PCs, which bypasses the need for high-end hardware. Which mini PC brands are reliable? Some of the most reliable mini PC brands are Minisforum, Beelink, GMKtec, and Geekom. Of course Apple’s Mac minis are also excellent computers if you prefer using macOS. Brands such as Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell all make high-quality smaller-footprint PCs, but they might not fill the same niche and/or they are typically more expensive.
